q: Why does water have a much higher boiling point than hydrogen sulfide?
expect: Water molecules experience hydrogen bonding (H bonded to O), an unusually strong dipole-dipole interaction, while H2S molecules do not; the extra attraction needs additional energy to separate H2O molecules, so water boils at 373 K (100 C) versus about -60 C for H2S (printed as 233 K; the [Note] corrects this to 213 K).

q: What happens to a system at equilibrium when more reactant is added?
expect: By Le Chatelier's principle the stressed equilibrium shifts to reduce the stress: adding reactant makes the reaction shift toward products (e.g. adding H2 to N2 + 3H2 <=> 2NH3 shifts it toward NH3) until equilibrium is re-established.
note: Re-targeted from Chemistry 1e 13.4. Beginning Chemistry 13.4 states the principle and the added-reactant case (line 19) with Example 13.4.1 (N2 + 3H2 <=> 2NH3, H2 added -> toward products). 'Chatelier' now occurs only in this file (9 hits), so the old distractor list no longer applies. The section says K_eq changes only with temperature (line 107) but does not explicitly say K is unchanged when reactant is added, so the expect no longer asserts that.

q: How do you calculate the pH of a buffer from the concentrations of the weak acid and its conjugate base?
expect: Use the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation: pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]), where [A-] is the concentration of the conjugate base and [HA] that of the weak acid. It comes from rearranging the acidity-constant expression (pKa = -log Ka). When the two concentrations are equal, log 1 = 0 and pH = pKa; each tenfold excess of base over acid raises the pH by one unit. Equivalently, log([A-]/[HA]) = pH - pKa gives the ratio of the two forms at a known pH (for example, acetic acid, pKa 4.76, at pH 7.3 has [A-]/[HA] = 10^2.54 = 3.5 x 10^2). A buffer is a weak acid together with its conjugate base (such as acetic acid and sodium acetate), which resists changes in pH.
note: Formerly a calculation question answered by Chemistry 1e 14.6 (Buffers), then labelled unanswerable (NEAR-MISS) when that book was removed; re-labelled answerable when organic chapter 20 was transcribed. 20-3 line 26 gives the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation, line 32 rearranges it, line 34 explains it (pH = pKa when [A-] = [HA]), and lines 36-40 work acetic acid at pH 7.3. The source prints the equation as 'pH = + log(...)', dropping pKa; the corpus corrects it in place with a [Note: ...], so an answer giving pH = + log([A-]/[HA]) has been misled by the misprint. The section applies the equation to dissociation at a given pH rather than calling it a buffer calculation; introductory 12-8-Buffers supplies what a buffer is (qualitatively, with HC2H3O2/NaC2H3O2). Likely false positives: introductory 13-6-Some-Special-Types-of-Equilibria (pH of a weak acid alone, ICE chart), 20-2 (Ka and pKa of carboxylic acids), 26-2 (amino acids and the equation, once transcribed).

q: What is the coordination number of the cobalt ion in [Co(en)3]3+?
expect: Six. Each ethylenediamine (en) ligand is bidentate (chelating): it binds the metal through the lone pairs on its two amine nitrogen atoms. The coordination number counts the ligand donor sites (atoms) bound to the metal, not the ligands, so three en ligands give 3 x 2 = 6. [Co(en)3]3+ (tris(ethylenediamine)cobalt(III)) is accordingly octahedral: the book treats six-coordinate complexes as octahedral and lists [Co(en)3]3+ among octahedral complexes of bidentate ligands, a tris-chelate showing only Lambda/Delta isomerism. 6 is also the coordination number Werner established for Co3+. Answering 3 (the number of ligands) is wrong.

q: What is the difference between accuracy and precision?
expect: Accuracy (or bias) is how close a result is to the 'true' or expected result. It is expressed as an absolute error e = x - mu (x the experimental result, mu the expected result) or a percent relative error %e_r = (x - mu)/mu x 100; because the true value is rarely known, it is judged against an accepted value, e.g. a standard reference material. Precision is a measure of the trial-to-trial variability when a sample is analysed several times: the closer the individual results agree, the more precise they are. It is reported as an absolute standard deviation s = sqrt(sum (Xi - Xbar)^2/(n - 1)) or a relative standard deviation s_r = s/Xbar. Precision does not imply accuracy: a tightly clustered set of results is not necessarily more accurate (Figure 1.4.2, potassium in serum), and 'neither set of results may be accurate'.

Line 41 lists both among a method's figures of merit. The 'more detailed treatment' it points to, Appendix 1 (analchem 35-1), is an empty stub. q: What is the law of definite proportions?
expect: The law of definite proportions (also called the law of constant composition), from Joseph Proust's experiments: all samples of a pure compound contain the same elements in the same proportion by mass. Example: different samples of isooctane all have a carbon-to-hydrogen mass ratio of 5.33:1 (Table 2.1.1: 14.82 g C/2.78 g H, 22.33 g/4.19 g, 19.40 g/3.64 g). The converse is not true: samples with the same mass ratio are not necessarily the same substance. Dalton's atomic theory accounts for it (the atoms of the elements in a compound always exist in the same ratio). It is distinct from the law of multiple proportions (when two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in a ratio of small whole numbers).

q: How do you calculate the average atomic mass of an element from its isotopes?
expect: The atomic mass is a weighted average: multiply each isotope's mass by its fractional occurrence (decimal abundance) and add the products. E.g. boron, about 20% B-10 and 80% B-11: 0.20 x 10 u + 0.80 x 11 u = 10.8 u.

q: What is Hess's law?
expect: Hess's law: when chemical equations are combined algebraically, their enthalpy changes combine in the same way. Reversing a reaction changes the sign of deltaH, and taking a multiple of a reaction multiplies deltaH by the same factor, so deltaH of a target reaction is the sum of the deltaH values of steps that add up to it.

q: What does the photoelectric effect demonstrate about the nature of light?
expect: That light behaves as a stream of particles (photons), each carrying a quantum of energy E = h nu, and not only as a wave (wave-particle duality). The observations: electrons are ejected from a metal only above a threshold frequency nu0, however intense the light; above it their kinetic energy rises linearly with frequency and does not depend on intensity, while the number of electrons (the current) is proportional to intensity; emission is practically instantaneous. Classical wave theory predicted the opposite (energy carried by light depends on its amplitude, so brighter light should give faster electrons). Einstein (1905): one photon is absorbed by one electron, so KE_max = h nu - Phi, where Phi is the work function (binding energy of the electron to the metal); raising the intensity only raises the number of photons and hence of electrons. The slope of KE against frequency is Planck's constant. A wave model cannot explain it because the energy would be spread over all the surface atoms. Millikan confirmed Einstein's theory in 1916.

q: Why does ionization energy generally increase from left to right across a period?

note: Re-targeted from Chemistry 1e 6.5 (was a distractor). Beginning Chemistry 8.6 explains the increasing nuclear charge across a row (line 22, for atomic radius) and that IE increases as electrons are drawn closer (line 59), with Figure 8.6.2 and Example 8.6.2. q: How do you calculate the formal charge on an atom in a Lewis structure?
expect: Formal charge = (number of valence electrons in the free, neutral atom) - (number of electrons the bonded atom owns), where the electrons it owns = half the bonding electrons + all the nonbonding electrons. So FC = valence electrons - (bonding electrons)/2 - nonbonding electrons. For example, the sulfur in dimethyl sulfoxide owns 5 electrons (one from each of three single bonds plus a lone pair) against 6 for a free sulfur atom, so its formal charge is +1, and the oxygen has -1; the nitrogen in ammonia owns 5, the same as a free N atom, so its formal charge is 0. Formal charges are a bookkeeping device, not actual ionic charges.
note: Formerly a calculation question answered by Chemistry 1e 7.4 (Formal Charges and Resonance), then labelled unanswerable when that book was removed; re-labelled answerable because organic chapter 2 now covers it. 02-3 line 26 states the rule in words and lines 28-30 give the formula; lines 18 and 22 work ammonia's nitrogen (0) and dimethyl sulfoxide's sulfur (+1) and oxygen (-1); line 14 calls formal charges electron bookkeeping, and Table 2.3.1 summarises common formal charges for C, N, O, S and P. Likely false positives: 02-9-Predicting-Acid-Base-Reactions-from-pKa-Values and 02-14/02-15 (mention formal charge without the method), and introductory 09-4-Covalent-Bonds and 09-6-Violations-of-the-Octet-Rule (Lewis structures, no formal charge).

q: How does VSEPR theory predict the shape of a molecule with lone pairs on the central atom?
expect: Count the electron groups (bonds of any order count as one; lone pairs count) on the central atom to get the electron group geometry; the molecular shape describes only the positions of the atoms. E.g. NH3 has four groups (tetrahedral) but is trigonal pyramidal; H2O has four groups but is bent; GeF2 (three groups, two bonded) is bent.

q: What is lattice energy and what does the Born-Haber cycle do?
expect: Lattice energy U is the energy required to separate one mole of an ionic solid into its gaseous ions (MaXb(s) -> a M^b+(g) + b X^a-(g)); defined this way it is always positive (endothermic). The reverse, the energy released when the gaseous ions form the solid, is the energy of crystallization, so U = -E_cryst (some texts use that sign convention). It measures the strength of the forces between the ions: it decreases as the ionic radii increase and is much larger for doubly charged ions (Table 7.7.1.1: LiF 1036, NaCl 786, KI 649, MgF2 2957 kJ/mol). It cannot be measured directly. q: How is bond order calculated in molecular orbital theory?
expect: Bond order = 1/2 x (number of electrons in bonding MOs - number of electrons in antibonding MOs); core electrons can be ignored because they contribute nothing. Fill the MO energy-level diagram (lowest first, Pauli and Hund), then count. Examples: H2 (sigma1s)^2: (2 - 0)/2 = 1; H2+ (sigma1s)^1: (1 - 0)/2 = 1/2; He2+ (sigma1s)^2(sigma*1s)^1: (2 - 1)/2 = 1/2; H2^2- and He2 (sigma1s)^2(sigma*1s)^2: (2 - 2)/2 = 0, predicted unstable; O2: (10 - 6)/2 = 2 counting all bonding/antibonding electrons (or (8 - 4)/2 with valence MOs only), with two unpaired electrons (paramagnetic). Bond orders 1, 2, 3 correspond to single, double and triple bonds; a higher bond order means a stronger, shorter bond, and a bond order of 0 means the species should not exist.

q: How is the half-life of a first-order chemical reaction related to its rate constant?
expect: For a first-order reaction the half-life is a constant, independent of the starting concentration, and inversely proportional to the rate constant: t1/2 = ln 2/k = 0.693/k (equivalently k = 0.693/t1/2). It follows from the integrated first-order rate law ln[A] = ln[A]o - kt (or [A] = [A]o e^(-kt)): setting [A] = [A]o/2 gives ln(1/2) = -k t1/2. The sources do not print t1/2 = 0.693/k as such, so a good answer shows this one-step derivation; it matches the radioactive-decay form amount remaining = initial x e^(-0.693 t/t1/2), radioactive decay being a first-order process. After each half-life half of the remaining reactant is gone (1/2, 1/4, 1/8 ...; a 120 s half-life leaves 25% after 240 s and 12.5% after 360 s).

q: What is a Lewis acid?
expect: A Lewis acid is a substance that accepts an electron pair (a Lewis base donates one); the donated pair is then shared between them in a covalent bond. Examples are H+, metal cations such as Mg2+, group 3A compounds such as BF3 and AlCl3, and transition-metal compounds such as TiCl4, FeCl3, ZnCl2 and SnCl4.

q: What does the sign of the Gibbs free energy change tell you about a process?
expect: At constant temperature and pressure the sign of Delta G (G = H - TS, Delta G = Delta H - T Delta S) gives the direction of spontaneous change. Delta G < 0: the process is spontaneous (favourable, exergonic: energy is released; favourable equilibrium constant). Delta G > 0: it does not occur spontaneously as written (endergonic) and can only be driven by coupling it to a process with a negative Delta G; the reverse process is spontaneous. Delta G = 0: the system is at equilibrium. Because of the -T Delta S term the sign can change with temperature: NH3(g) + HCl(g) -> NH4Cl(s) has Delta H = -176.2 kJ and Delta S = -0.285 kJ/K, so Delta G = -91.3 kJ at 298 K, but above about 618 K Delta G is positive and NH4Cl decomposes instead. It is the sign of Delta rG under the actual conditions (Delta rG = Delta rG deg + RT ln Q), not of Delta G deg, that decides. How fast the process goes is a separate matter, set by the activation energy.

q: How is elemental sulfur mined from underground deposits?

The sulfur is very pure (99.5%, up to 99.9%). The process, in use since the 1890s, is useful for deposits under water or quicksand; most of the sulfur it produces is used to make sulfuric acid by the contact process.

q: What is the mechanism of the aldol condensation?
expect: The aldol reaction is a base-catalyzed carbonyl condensation between two aldehyde or ketone molecules that have an alpha hydrogen. Base removes an acidic alpha hydrogen from one partner to give an enolate ion, the nucleophilic donor; the enolate adds to the electrophilic carbonyl carbon of the second partner (the acceptor), so the donor undergoes an alpha substitution and the acceptor a nucleophilic addition. Protonation of the resulting alkoxide gives a beta-hydroxy aldehyde or ketone (acetaldehyde gives 3-hydroxybutanal, 'aldol'), and the base is regenerated. The steps are reversible: the equilibrium favours the product for RCH2CHO aldehydes but the reactants for R2CHCHO aldehydes and most ketones. On heating with acid or base the aldol product dehydrates to a conjugated enone (the 'condensation', losing water): in base an enolate expels the neighbouring -OH in an E1cB reaction; in acid the enol forms, the -OH is protonated and water leaves by E1 or E2. Removing the water drives the equilibrium toward the product.

q: What is a disproportionation reaction?
expect: Disproportionation occurs when a species reacts with itself to produce two or more stable products; it is a redox reaction in which the same element is both oxidized and reduced. q: if electrons have a wavelength then why doesnt a softball i throw have one?? or does it

q: my prof keeps saying real gases stop acting ideal at high pressure and low temp but why exactly does that happen
expect: The ideal gas law treats the particles as having no volume and exerting no forces on each other. That holds at low pressure, where the finite volume of the particles and the intermolecular attractions have little impact. At higher pressures (higher densities) the molecules are close together, so (1) their own volume is a significant part of the container, and the volume actually available is V - nb, not V; and (2) attractions between molecules reduce the net force of their impacts on the wall, so the real pressure is less than ideal (corrected by an^2/V^2) - the van der Waals equation (P + n^2a/V^2)(V - nb) = nRT. The compressibility factor Z = PV/nRT measures the deviation: Z = 1 for an ideal gas, and every real gas approaches Z = 1 at sufficiently low pressure. Low temperature makes the attractions matter more: at high temperatures the isotherms approach those of an ideal gas, while at low temperatures (below the critical temperature) compressing the gas makes it condense to a liquid; van der Waals traced 'the root cause of condensation of gases into liquids at lower temperatures' to 'the attractive interactions between the molecules'.

q: How many radial nodes does an orbital have, and how many does a 3s orbital have?
expect: The number of radial nodes is n - l - 1 (inorgchem writes it n - 1 - l). A 3s orbital (n = 3, l = 0) has 3 - 1 - 0 = 2 radial nodes. Radial nodes are spherical surfaces where the radial part of the wavefunction R_n,l(r), and so the radial probability 4 pi r^2 R^2, is zero (other than at r = 0 and r = infinity); they are distinct from angular nodes, of which there are l. Pattern: 1s 0, 2s 1, 3s 2, 4s 3; 2p 0, 3p 1, 4p 2; 3d 0, 4d 1. The total number of nodes is n - 1.

q: why does lead usually form Pb2+ instead of losing all 4 of its valence electrons like you'd expect for group 14?
expect: This is the inert pair effect. Heavier post-transition p-block metals commonly have two stable oxidation states, one from losing all the ns and np valence electrons (Pb4+) and one two lower (Pb2+), as if the ns^2 pair were inert, and the lower state is increasingly preferred going down a group; Pb4+ is a potent oxidant and lead prefers +2 (it forms PbO and PbS). The book stresses that the name is a misnomer: the ns electrons do not become significantly lower in energy down a group. Instead, bond energies decrease as bond lengths increase down the group, while the ionization energy needed to remove the ns^2 pair does not fall, so for the heavy elements the energy gained by forming two extra bonds no longer pays for ionizing the ns electrons and the lower oxidation state is more stable. (Worked for group 13: Tl-Cl 372.8 vs B-Cl 536 kJ/mol, while M+ -> M3+ costs about 4500-4900 kJ/mol from Al to Tl.)

q: In the van der Waals equation, what do the n^2a/V^2 and nb terms each correct for?
expect: In (P + n^2a/V^2)(V - nb) = nRT: the n^2a/V^2 term corrects the pressure for intermolecular attractions. Attractions reduce the net force of the molecules hitting the wall, so the real gas exerts less pressure than an ideal one, and an^2/V^2 is added back (P = P_real + an^2/V^2); it goes as n^2/V^2 because the number of attractive interactions grows as 1/V^2. The nb term corrects the volume for the finite size of the molecules: b is the excluded volume per mole (hard spheres of diameter sigma, b = (2/3) pi sigma^3 N0), so the volume actually available to the molecules is V - nb. a and b depend on the substance (e.g. N2 a = 1.370 L^2 bar/mol^2, b = 0.0387 L/mol; H2O 5.536 and 0.03049); with a = b = 0 the equation reduces to PV = nRT.

q: why does water curve up the sides of a glass tube and climb up a thin straw-like tube, but mercury bulges up in the middle and goes down instead?
expect: Water's adhesive forces with glass are strong (stronger than its cohesion), so in a thin glass tube it shows capillary rise and an upwardly curved meniscus. Mercury has very strong cohesive forces, stronger than its adhesion to glass, so it shows capillary depression: its surface is pushed down in the tube and the meniscus curves the other way.

q: What is the boiling point of benzene in Denver, where atmospheric pressure is 83.4 kPa? Benzene's normal boiling point is 80.1 °C and its enthalpy of vaporization is 30.8 kJ/mol.

The normal boiling point is where the vapour pressure equals 1 atm (101.325 kPa), so P1 = 101.325 kPa at T1 = 80.1 + 273.15 = 353.25 K, and benzene boils in Denver when its vapour pressure reaches 83.4 kPa. 1/T2 = 1/T1 - (R/Delta H_vap) ln(P2/P1) = 1/353.25 - (8.3145/30 800) x ln(83.4/101.325) = 2.8309 x 10^-3 + 5.26 x 10^-5 = 2.8834 x 10^-3 K^-1, so T2 = 346.8 K, about 73.7 deg C (some 6 deg C below its normal boiling point).

q: On a cold day I can hear liquid sloshing inside a CO2 fire extinguisher, but on a really hot summer day it sounds empty. Whats going on?
expect: It is the critical temperature. For CO2, T_c is about 31 deg C (304.1 K; critical pressure 7.37 MPa = 73.7 bar). Below T_c the compressed CO2 in the extinguisher is partly liquid in equilibrium with its vapour, so on a cold day you hear liquid sloshing. The critical temperature is the highest temperature at which a gas-liquid transition can occur: above it there is no liquid-gas phase transition at any pressure, and the CO2 is a single supercritical fluid (liquid-like at high pressure, gas-like at lower pressure). On a hot day above 31 deg C there is therefore no separate liquid to slosh. At the critical point the liquid and vapour phases become alike and coalesce.

q: how come candle wax just gets soft and gooey gradually when you heat it, instead of melting at one exact temperature like ice does?
expect: Candle wax is an amorphous (noncrystalline) solid: it is made of large hydrocarbon molecules whose arrangement lacks an ordered, repeating pattern. In a crystalline solid such as ice every particle of the same type is held by the same forces, so all the attractions need the same energy to break and the solid has a precise melting temperature. In an amorphous solid the molecules are structurally nonequivalent, so some attractions are weaker than others: on heating the weakest break first and the stronger ones only at higher temperatures, so the material softens gradually over a range of temperatures instead of melting sharply.

Thus amorphous materials soften over a range of temperatures'). Grep 'candle' 1 hit (07-2 line 23); 'amorphous' 30 hits in 6 files. q: What is the coordination number of an atom in a BCC metal versus an FCC metal, and how many atoms does each unit cell contain?
expect: BCC (body-centred cubic): atoms at the eight corners and one in the centre of the cube; each atom touches four atoms in the layer above and four in the layer below, so the coordination number is 8; the unit cell contains 8 x 1/8 + 1 = 2 atoms; atoms fill about 68% of the volume (e.g. K, Ba, Cr, Mo, W, Fe). FCC (face-centred cubic, equivalent to cubic closest packing): atoms at the corners and the centres of the six faces; each atom touches 6 in its own layer, 3 above and 3 below, so the coordination number is 12; the unit cell contains 8 x 1/8 + 6 x 1/2 = 4 atoms; 74% of the volume is filled (e.g. Al, Cu, Pb). (For comparison, simple cubic: coordination number 6, 1 atom per cell, 52%.)

q: If dissolving stuff is supposed to be spontaneous, how does an instant cold pack get cold? Shouldn't it give off heat?
expect: Spontaneous does not mean exothermic: energy (the first law) alone does not decide whether a process happens. The book's own example: KNO3 dissolves in water spontaneously, but the solution gets cold, while KOH dissolves spontaneously and the solution gets hot. A cold pack works the same way: the dissolving absorbs heat from its surroundings (endothermic, Delta H > 0), yet it still happens because it increases the entropy (mixing gives more possible arrangements, the driving force for mixing). At constant temperature and pressure the criterion is Delta G = Delta H - T Delta S <= 0, so a positive Delta H is outweighed when T Delta S is larger. The sources do not describe cold packs or name the salt in them.

q: How does soap actually get grease off your hands?
expect: A soap molecule is the sodium or potassium salt of a long-chain fatty acid, and its two ends behave differently: the ionic carboxylate head is hydrophilic (attracted to water), while the long hydrocarbon tail is nonpolar and hydrophobic, avoiding water and dissolving in oils. In water, soap molecules cluster into spherical micelles, with the tails tangled together inside and the ionic heads on the surface facing the water. Grease and oil droplets are coated by the hydrophobic tails in the centre of the micelles, which carries them into the water so they can be rinsed away. (In hard water, soaps form insoluble calcium and magnesium salts - scum - which synthetic alkylbenzenesulfonate detergents avoid.)
note: Formerly a distractor question answered by Chemistry 1e 11-6 (Soaps and Detergents), then labelled unanswerable (NEAR-MISS) when that book was removed; re-labelled answerable when organic chapter 27 was transcribed. orgchem 27-2 line 16 gives the hydrophilic carboxylate head and hydrophobic tail, line 18 the micelle and how grease is solubilized and rinsed away (Figure 27.2.1, line 20), line 23 hard water and synthetic detergents. q: Can I just write the rate law straight from the coefficients in the balanced equation?
expect: No. The rate law cannot be predicted by looking at the balanced chemical equation; it must be determined by experiment (measuring how the rate depends on the concentrations, e.g. by initial-rate or full concentration-time methods such as stopped-flow with spectrophotometry). Example: Cl2(g) + CO(g) -> Cl2CO(g) has the experimental rate law rate = k[Cl2]^(3/2)[CO], three-halves order in Cl2 and first order in CO (overall 5/2), although both coefficients are 1. The orders reflect the mechanism, a sequence of elementary reactions, not the overall stoichiometry, and even a measured rate law does not imply a unique mechanism. Don't confuse this with the equilibrium-constant expression, where the coefficients do become exponents.

q: If making ammonia is exothermic, why do factories run the Haber process so hot instead of at low temperature where the yield is better?
expect: Because the low-temperature yield is useless if the reaction is too slow. N2 + 3H2 <-> 2NH3 is exothermic (ΔH_rxn = -91.8 kJ/mol), so K falls as temperature rises (e.g. K = 0.039 at 800 K) and the best equilibrium yield would be at low temperature and high pressure (4 mol of gas become 2, so Le Chatelier favours high pressure). But below about 300 °C, where the equilibrium yield would be relatively high, the reaction is too slow to be of commercial use. So plants compromise: a mixed-oxide Fe2O3/K2O catalyst lets the reaction go at a useful rate at 400-530 °C and 130-330 atm, where NH3 formation is less unfavourable than at still higher temperatures; only part of the N2/H2 is converted per pass, the NH3 is condensed out as a liquid and the unreacted gases are recycled until conversion is complete.

Student phrasing. 31-10 line 20 gives the whole argument: exothermic so K decreases with temperature, 'maximum yield ... at as low a temperature and as high a pressure as possible. Unfortunately, at temperatures less than approximately 300°C ... the reaction is too slow to be of any commercial use', hence the Fe2O3/K2O catalyst at 400-530 °C; line 18 ΔH_rxn = -91.8 kJ/mol; Figure 31.10.1 caption (line 22) gives 400-530 °C and 130-330 atm; line 28 gives K = 0.039 at 800 K and the condense-and-recycle strategy; Figure 31.10.2 caption (line 30) the plant layout. q: In the Boltzmann equation S = k ln W, what does W stand for, and what is k?

q: How can you estimate the boiling point of water from standard enthalpy and entropy data?

q: How do you balance a redox reaction in basic solution using the half-reaction method?

q: In a galvanic cell, which electrode is the anode, and which way do electrons and salt-bridge ions move?
expect: The anode is the half cell where oxidation occurs, and the cathode is where reduction occurs. q: What voltage does a zinc concentration cell produce with 0.10 M Zn2+ at the anode and 0.50 M Zn2+ at the cathode?
expect: About +0.021 V (20.7 mV). Both electrodes are Zn in Zn2+ (electrodes of the first kind), so E° for the overall reaction is 0 and only the concentrations matter. E_cell = E_cathode - E_anode, each from the Nernst equation E = E° - (0.05916/n) log(1/[Zn2+]) with n = 2 and E° = -0.763 V: E_cathode = -0.763 - 0.02958 log(1/0.50) = -0.7719 V, E_anode = -0.763 - 0.02958 log(1/0.10) = -0.7926 V, so E_cell = (0.05916/2) log(0.50/0.10) = 0.02958 × 0.699 = 0.0207 V. Equivalently, for Zn2+(0.50 M, cathode) -> Zn2+(0.10 M, anode), E = 0 - (0.05916/2) log(0.10/0.50) = +0.0207 V. Positive, so the cell runs spontaneously with reduction in the more concentrated half-cell. (Strictly the books write the Nernst equation in activities; using concentrations is the approximation 22-4 also makes in part b.)

q: What is passivation, and why doesn't aluminum corrode away even though it is a reactive metal?
expect: Passivation is protection of a reactive metal by a thin layer of its own oxide (or other solid oxidation product) that coats the surface and seals the bulk metal off from further reaction with oxygen. Such layers are 'said to be passivating', and the resulting anodic passivation is a kinetic, not thermodynamic, stabilization: the metal is still thermodynamically unstable to oxidation, but the coating stops the reaction. Be and Mg, for example, can be used in air because their initial oxidation gives a thin passivating oxide layer. Aluminum is the same case: the corrosion of aluminum (and copper) forms a protective barrier on the surface that protects it from further reaction with the environment, whereas iron's rust flakes off and does not protect it.

q: my lab instructor said you can store any acid in a glass bottle except hydrofluoric acid. why is HF different?
expect: Because HF reacts with the silica in glass. Glass is SiO2, and HF converts it to gaseous silicon tetrafluoride: SiO2 + 4 HF(aq) -> 2 H2O + SiF4(g), so 'hydrofluoric acid can etch glass'. HF is the only aqueous acid that silicon reacts with, attributed to formation of the stable SiF6^2- ion. Other acids (HCl, HNO3, H2SO4) have no such reaction with SiO2, so glass bottles are fine for them; this holds even though HF is the weakest of the hydrohalic acids, so it is not about acid strength.

q: Why does graphite conduct electricity while diamond does not?
expect: Graphite's carbons are trigonal planar (sp2) and bonded in flat graphene sheets by sigma bonds plus a delocalized π-bond network; that delocalized π system forms a half-filled valence band of π-type orbitals, which is responsible for graphite's good electrical conductivity (its π valence band and π* conduction band overlap, leaving no band gap). Diamond is all-sigma: every carbon is tetrahedral and held by single (σ) bonds, so there are no delocalized electrons and a large band gap, and it is a poor electrical conductor.

q: Why is [Fe(CN)6]4- a low-spin complex while [Fe(H2O)6]2+ is high-spin, and how many unpaired electrons does each have?
expect: Both are octahedral Fe(II), d6. Whether a d^n ion is high- or low-spin depends on the octahedral splitting Δo versus the pairing energy Π. Water is a weak-field ligand (a π donor, low in the spectrochemical series): for Fe(OH2)6^2+, Δo = 10,000 cm^-1 is smaller than Π = 17,600 cm^-1, so it costs less to put electrons in eg than to pair them, giving high spin t2g^4 eg^2 with 4 unpaired electrons (spin-only μ = √(4·6) = 4.90 BM). Cyanide is a strong-field π-acceptor ligand near the top of the spectrochemical series (CO > CN- > phen > NO2- > SCN-; π acceptors give the largest splittings), so Δo exceeds the pairing energy and the six electrons pair up in t2g: low spin t2g^6, 0 unpaired electrons (diamagnetic).

q: why can 2-butene have cis and trans versions but butane cant?
expect: Rotation around a C=C double bond would require breaking the pi bond (the sideways overlap of the p orbitals), an estimated 350 kJ/mol, so it doesn't happen. The two methyl groups of 2-butene are therefore locked either on the same side of the double bond (cis-2-butene) or on opposite sides (trans-2-butene); the two can't interconvert and are different, isolable compounds (cis-trans stereoisomers). Butane has only single (sigma) bonds, around which rotation is essentially free (the barrier in ethane is only 12 kJ/mol), so its different arrangements are interconverting conformations of one compound, not isomers. Cis-trans isomerism also needs each double-bond carbon to carry two different groups.

q: how do i read the splitting pattern in a 1H NMR spectrum? like what does a triplet next to a quartet mean
expect: Spin-spin splitting: a proton's signal is split by the spins of protons on neighbouring carbons. By the n + 1 rule, protons with n equivalent neighbouring protons show n + 1 peaks, so a triplet (1 : 2 : 1) means two neighbouring protons (a CH2 next door) and a quartet (1 : 3 : 3 : 1) means three (a CH3 next door). A triplet paired with a quartet that share the same coupling constant J is the signature of an ethyl group, CH3CH2-: in bromoethane the CH3 is a triplet at 1.68 delta and the CH2Br a quartet at 3.42 delta, both with J = 7 Hz. Equivalent protons don't split each other, protons more than two carbons apart don't usually couple, and multiplets with the same J come from protons that are coupled to each other (adjacent in the molecule).
note: Formerly unanswerable (NEAR-MISS); re-labelled when organic chapter 13 was transcribed. q: whats the difference between SN1 and SN2 reactions and how do i know which one happens
expect: SN2: one step in which the nucleophile attacks from the side opposite (180 degrees from) the leaving group, inverting the configuration; second-order kinetics, rate = k[RX][Nu]; slowed by steric bulk, so it is best for methyl and primary substrates, slow for secondary ones, and tertiary substrates don't react this way. SN1: the substrate first dissociates to a carbocation in a slow rate-limiting step, then the nucleophile adds quickly; first-order kinetics, rate = k[RX]; the planar carbocation gives substantial racemization (usually with a small excess of inversion, from ion pairs); best for tertiary, allylic and benzylic substrates. Which one happens: SN1 is favored by tertiary, allylic or benzylic substrates, good leaving groups, nonbasic nucleophiles and protic solvents; SN2 by primary substrates, good leaving groups, good nucleophiles and polar aprotic solvents.
note: Formerly unanswerable (NEAR-MISS); re-labelled when organic chapter 11 was transcribed. q: When HBr adds to propene, which carbon does the bromine end up on, and why (Markovnikov's rule)?
expect: The bromine ends up on the middle carbon (C2), giving 2-bromopropane rather than 1-bromopropane. Markovnikov's rule: in the addition of HX to an alkene, the H attaches to the carbon with fewer alkyl substituents (here the CH2 end) and the X to the carbon with more alkyl substituents. The reason is that the addition goes through a carbocation: adding H+ to the CH2 end gives a secondary carbocation, which is more stable than the primary carbocation that adding it to C2 would give (stability order tertiary > secondary > primary > methyl, from inductive effects and hyperconjugation), and the more stable carbocation forms faster (Hammond postulate). Bromide then bonds to that carbocation.
note: Formerly unanswerable (NEAR-MISS); the label went stale when organic chapter 7 was transcribed. 07-8 line 18 states Markovnikov's rule and line 30 restates it in terms of the more highly substituted carbocation; line 32 applies it (2-methylpropene gives the tertiary rather than the primary carbocation). 07-9 line 17 and its figure give the carbocation stability order, and 07-10 (Hammond postulate) explains why the more stable carbocation forms faster. The book's examples use 2-methylpropene, 1-methylcyclohexene and 2-pentene, not propene, so a correct answer applies the rule: H to C1, secondary carbocation, 2-bromopropane. q: How do you use Hückel's 4n+2 rule to decide whether a ring like cyclooctatetraene is aromatic?
expect: Hückel's rule: a molecule is aromatic only if it has a planar, monocyclic system of conjugation (a p orbital on every ring atom) and a total of 4n + 2 pi electrons (2, 6, 10, 14, ...). Planar, conjugated rings with 4n pi electrons (4, 8, 12, ...) are antiaromatic. Count the pi electrons and check the geometry: benzene has 6 (n = 1) and is aromatic; cyclobutadiene has 4 and is antiaromatic. Cyclooctatetraene has 8 pi electrons, a 4n number, so it is not aromatic: it avoids antiaromaticity by being tub-shaped rather than planar, its pi electrons are localized in four double bonds (single bonds 147 pm, double bonds 134 pm), it reacts like an open-chain polyene, and its 1H NMR signal is at 5.78 delta, an alkene value. The reason is MO theory: cyclic conjugated systems have one lowest MO and then degenerate pairs, so 4n + 2 electrons exactly fill the bonding levels. (Adding two electrons gives the cyclooctatetraene dianion, which has 10 pi electrons and is planar and aromatic.)
note: Formerly unanswerable (NEAR-MISS); re-labelled when organic chapter 15 was transcribed. 15-3 line 18 states the Hückel 4n + 2 rule and defines antiaromatic; lines 22-34 work cyclobutadiene (4, antiaromatic), benzene (6, aromatic) and cyclooctatetraene (8, tub-shaped, localized double bonds); line 38 gives the bond lengths and the 5.78 delta NMR signal; line 40 gives the MO explanation. 15-4 Exercise 15.4.2 (line 48) adds the aromatic, flat C8H8^2- dianion, and 15-7 line 51 notes cyclooctatetraene's nonaromatic NMR shift. q: how do i assign R or S to a chiral carbon? i keep messing up the priority rules
expect: Rank the four groups on the chirality center with the sequence (Cahn-Ingold-Prelog) rules. Rule 1: the atom directly attached with the higher atomic number ranks higher (Br > Cl > S > P > O > N > C > 2H > 1H; a heavier isotope ranks above a lighter one). Rule 2: if the first atoms tie, compare the atoms further out (second, third, fourth) until the first difference, so ethyl outranks methyl. Rule 3: multiple-bonded atoms count as the same number of single-bonded atoms (C=O counts as a carbon bonded to two oxygens). Then orient the molecule so the lowest-ranked group (4) points away from you and trace 1 -> 2 -> 3: clockwise is R (rectus; a right turn of a steering wheel), counterclockwise is S (sinister). The sign of optical rotation, (+) or (-), is not related to R or S.
note: Formerly unanswerable; the label went stale when organic chapter 5 was transcribed. q: Why are octahedral copper(II) complexes usually distorted, with two long axial bonds (the Jahn-Teller effect)?
expect: Cu(II) is d9, and in an octahedral field that leaves the degenerate eg pair unequally occupied (three electrons in two orbitals). When degenerate orbitals are unequally occupied, lowering the symmetry splits them, so two electrons go lower and one higher, a net decrease in energy: the complex distorts (the Jahn-Teller effect). Elongating the two axial bonds (a tetragonal distortion) slightly lowers the orbitals with z character (dz2, dxz, dyz) and raises the others, keeping the barycentre. Strong distortions occur only when the unequal occupancy is in eg, which points at the ligands and governs σ bonding and bond length: high-spin d4, low-spin d7 and d9. Example: EXAFS on [Cu(OH2)6](BrO3)2 shows two Cu-O distances, 1.96(1) and 2.32(2) Å, about a 20% difference. The distortion also splits the d-d band and makes octahedral Cu(II) complexes labile by weakening the axial bonds.

q: Use the Debye-Hückel limiting law to calculate the mean activity coefficient of NaCl in a 0.010 M solution.

q: Derive the Michaelis-Menten equation and explain what Km means for an enzyme.
expect: Mechanism: E + S <-> ES (k1, k-1), ES -> E + P (k2). Apply the steady-state approximation to ES: d[ES]/dt = k1[E][S] - k-1[ES] - k2[ES] ≈ 0, with enzyme conservation [E]0 = [E] + [ES]. Solving gives [ES]ss = [E]0[S]/([S] + (k-1 + k2)/k1), so the rate is d[P]/dt = k2[ES]ss = k2[E]0[S]/([S] + K_M), the Michaelis-Menten equation, with K_M = (k-1 + k2)/k1, the Michaelis constant. At [S] >> K_M the rate becomes zero order, r_max = k2[E]0 (k2 is the turnover number); the Lineweaver-Burk form 1/r = (K_M/k2[E]0)(1/[S]) + 1/(k2[E]0) gives K_M/r_max as slope and 1/r_max as intercept. Meaning of K_M: it sets the substrate concentration at which the rate saturates; setting [S] = K_M gives r = r_max/2 (a consequence of the equation; the book does not state it in words).

q: What are the allowed energy levels for a particle in a one-dimensional box of length L?

q: How does the Krebs cycle produce ATP in the mitochondria?
expect: The citric acid (Krebs) cycle, the third stage of catabolism, runs inside mitochondria and oxidizes the acetyl group of acetyl CoA to two molecules of CO2 in an eight-step closed loop that regenerates oxaloacetate. It makes little ATP directly: its energy is captured mostly as the reduced coenzymes NADH and FADH2 (from the oxidations in steps 3, 4, 6 and 8), plus one GTP from succinyl CoA in step 5. The reduced coenzymes are reoxidized in the fourth stage, the electron-transport chain, which uses oxygen as the final electron acceptor; the energy released there drives the endergonic phosphorylation of ADP with hydrogen phosphate to ATP. That is also why the cycle depends on oxygen. The sources do not describe how the electron-transport chain itself makes ATP (no proton gradient or ATP synthase), so an answer must not add those details as sourced.

q: if an astronaut goes to the moon does her mass actually change or just her weight? whats the difference
expect: Only her weight changes. Mass is the absolute amount of matter in an object (measured in grams) and is fixed; weight is the gravitational force acting on that mass, W = m × g, where g is the acceleration due to gravity, so an object's weight depends on g wherever it is. On the moon g is smaller, so she weighs less but has the same mass. (The book says g 'varies subtly from location-to-location' on Earth; the moon's value, about one-sixth of Earth's, is not in the sources and must not be cited as sourced.) That is also why a balance actually measures weight and must be calibrated with standard masses to report mass.

q: Why does iodine barely dissolve in water but dissolve easily in a potassium iodide solution?
expect: Iodine is only slightly soluble in water (0.0013 mol/dm^3 at 25 °C; iodine and water molecules attract each other weakly), but in potassium iodide solution it dissolves freely because iodine molecules react reversibly with iodide ions to form the triiodide ion, I2 + I- <-> I3-, giving a dark red-brown solution. In Lewis terms I2 acts as a Lewis acid (a heavier element able to form hypervalent species) and I- as the Lewis base. As long as excess iodide is present, iodine goes into solution as I3-; once the iodide is used up, iodine precipitates as a dark grey solid.

q: How can diethyl ether be made from ethanol, and what is it mainly used for today?
expect: Diethyl ether is made industrially by the sulfuric-acid-catalyzed reaction of ethanol: acid protonates one ethanol molecule, and the oxygen of a second ethanol displaces water from it in an SN2 reaction, followed by loss of a proton. Uses: it has a long history as an anesthetic, but it fell out of favour because of its flammability and toxicity; today it is used mainly as a solvent, in industry and in the laboratory (with care, since ethers can form explosive peroxides).

q: is cooking an egg a physical change or a chemical change? and what about ice melting? how do you tell the difference
expect: A physical change alters one or more physical properties (e.g. a solid melting) without affecting the chemical composition of the matter, so ice melting into liquid water is a physical change. A chemical change demonstrates a chemical property: the composition changes and new forms of matter with new physical properties are made (e.g. a match burning). Frying an egg heats it until a chemical reaction occurs to cook it, so cooking an egg is a chemical change (the book notes that a lot of cooking involves chemical changes, e.g. bread dough becoming bread). Chemical changes are often accompanied by physical changes.
note: Beginning Chemistry 1.2: 'Physical Change' (line 66), 'Chemical Change' (line 74), Example 1.2.2c bread dough (line 88), and the 'Chemistry is Everywhere: In the Morning' box on frying eggs (line 187). The ice-melting figure caption (line 68) calls it a physical change. The [Note] at line 70 is only about figure numbering and does not affect the answer.

q: In science, what's the difference between a hypothesis, a theory, and a law? Isn't a theory just a guess?
expect: A hypothesis is an educated guess about how the natural universe works; to be scientific it must be testable (supported or refuted by experiment or observation), and it is often written as an if/then statement. A theory is a general statement that explains a large number of observations once enough evidence has been collected (e.g. 'all matter is composed of atoms'); it indicates an overwhelming amount of evidence, so it is not a mere guess - the everyday use of 'theory' to mean hypothesis is different from the scientific use. A law is a specific statement thought never to be violated by the natural universe, the highest understanding science has (e.g. the law of gravitation that all matter attracts all other matter).
note: Beginning Chemistry 1.3: hypothesis (lines 24, 26, 32), theory (line 38), law and the common-usage contrast (line 40). Tests a definitional contrast the student frames casually. Only 1.3 defines these terms.

q: Why is MgCl2 called magnesium chloride and not magnesium dichloride, when N2O3 gets prefixes and is called dinitrogen trioxide?
expect: Prefixes (mono-, di-, tri-, ...) are used only when naming molecular compounds, which form between nonmetals (e.g. N2O3, dinitrogen trioxide; SO2 sulfur dioxide). MgCl2 is an ionic compound (a metal with a nonmetal), and ionic compounds are named by combining the cation name and the anion name with no numerical prefixes, because the number of each ion is dictated by balancing the charges: one Mg^2+ needs two Cl^- ions. So MgCl2 is magnesium chloride, not magnesium dichloride. (Only polyatomic ions whose own names contain a prefix, like dichromate, keep it.)
note: Beginning Chemistry 3.5 line 134 states 'MgCl2 is magnesium chloride - not magnesium dichloride' and line 164 gives the metal/nonmetal test; 3.3 lines 32-40 give the prefix rules for binary molecular compounds (Table 3.3.2). The molecular-mass example of N2O3 is in 3.4 but naming is not. Distinct from q015 (Roman numerals).

q: how do i know if one metal will kick another metal out of a compound? like if i drop copper wire into silver nitrate solution does anything happen
expect: Use the activity series for cation replacement in single-replacement reactions: an element higher on the list replaces an element below it in a compound, but not one above it. Copper (Cu) is listed above silver (Ag), so copper replaces silver: a reaction occurs, giving copper nitrate and silver metal. (By contrast, gold is below hydrogen, so HNO3 + Au gives no reaction.) For halogens the periodic table plays the same role: a halogen higher in the column replaces one below it.
note: Beginning Chemistry 4.3: the activity series list (lines 66-89, Cu above Hg, Ag) and the rule at line 91; Examples 4.3.1-4.3.2. The book does not use Cu + AgNO3 itself, so the answer must apply the series. 'activity series' occurs only in 4.3 (9 hits), across both books.

q: Why do I have to convert grams to moles before I use the coefficients in a balanced equation? Can't I just use the grams directly?
expect: Because chemical equations are balanced in terms of moles (numbers of particles), not grams. The coefficients give mole equivalences (e.g. 2 mol H2 <=> 1 mol O2 <=> 2 mol H2O), so a given mass must first be converted to moles with its molar mass, then the mole ratio from the coefficients is applied, and then (for a mass-mass problem) the result is converted back to mass with the other substance's molar mass: mass -> mol -> mol -> mass.
note: Beginning Chemistry 5.5 line 22 ('chemical equations are not balanced in terms of grams; they are balanced in terms of moles') and line 108/162; 5.4 line 36 and line 100. The [Note] at 5.4 line 102 adds that gas volumes at the same T and P follow the mole ratio but 'Masses never do', consistent with this answer.

q: if an acid gives off H+ and H+ is just a proton, are there really bare protons floating around in the solution?
expect: No. An H^+ ion is a hydrogen atom that has lost its electron, i.e. simply a proton, but bare protons are not moving about in aqueous solution; the H^+ attaches to one or more water molecules. This is represented by the hydronium ion, H3O^+ (a proton attached to a water molecule), which is the more logical/chemically proper way to write the hydrogen ion in water, although H^+ and H3O^+ are often treated equivalently in equations (e.g. H^+ + OH^- -> H2O is equivalent to H3O^+ + OH^- -> 2H2O).
note: Beginning Chemistry 4.6 line 17 (hydronium definition) and lines 85-91 (the two equivalent net ionic equations); 12.2 line 15 repeats the point in the Arrhenius definition. 'hydronium' hits: 04-6 (2), 12-2 (1), 12-5 (1, a back-reference only).

q: I have a 250.0 g piece of pure gold. Using the textbook's density for gold, what volume does it occupy?
expect: Use the reciprocal of the density as the conversion factor (Table 2.6.1: gold 19.3 g/mL): 250.0 g x (1 mL / 19.3 g) = 12.95 mL, which to three significant figures (density has 3) is 13.0 mL (13.0 cm^3).
note: Beginning Chemistry 2.6, Table 2.6.1 (gold 19.3 g/mL, line 105) and the reciprocal-density method (lines 146-152, worked for 45.9 g of gold = 2.38 mL). Arithmetic: 250.0/19.3 = 12.953 -> 13.0. Context changed from the book's 45.9 g example.

q: A lab bench top measures 152.4 cm by 76.2 cm. What is its area in square meters, to the correct number of significant figures?
expect: Area = 152.4 cm x 76.2 cm = 11,612.88 cm^2. Convert with two factors of (1 m / 100 cm), one for each length unit: 11,612.88 cm^2 x (1 m/100 cm) x (1 m/100 cm) = 1.161288 m^2. The 1 and 100 are exact numbers, so significant figures are set by 76.2 (three): 1.16 m^2.
note: Beginning Chemistry 2.5: squared-unit conversions need two conversion factors (line 134), exact numbers don't affect sig figs (lines 217-225), and Example 2.5.5 (garden plot 36.7 cm x 128.8 cm = 0.473 m^2, line 235). Arithmetic: 152.4 x 76.2 = 11612.88; /10^4 = 1.161288 -> 1.16.

q: how many sig figs should these answers have: 12.51 + 3.2 - 0.006, and 4.52 x 0.0030?
expect: Addition/subtraction: limit to the rightmost column all numbers share. 12.51 + 3.2 - 0.006 = 15.704; 3.2 stops at the tenths place, so report 15.7 (first dropped digit 0, round down). Multiplication/division: limit to the fewest significant figures. 4.52 (three) x 0.0030 (two; leading zeros are not significant, the trailing zero after the decimal point is) = 0.01356, reported to two significant figures as 0.014 (first dropped digit 5 -> round up).
note: Beginning Chemistry 2.4: counting rules 3-4 (lines 60-61), the addition/subtraction rule (line 99), rounding rule (line 105), and the multiplication/division rule (line 133). Arithmetic: 12.51+3.2-0.006 = 15.704 -> 15.7; 4.52 x 0.0030 = 0.01356 -> 0.014.

q: How many moles and how many molecules of carbon dioxide are in 50.0 g of CO2?
expect: Molar mass of CO2 from the atomic masses (C 12.011, O 15.999): 12.011 + 2(15.999) = 44.009 g/mol. Moles: 50.0 g x (1 mol / 44.009 g) = 1.136 -> 1.14 mol CO2. Molecules: 1.136 mol x 6.022 x 10^23 molecules/mol = 6.84 x 10^23 molecules CO2.
note: Beginning Chemistry 5.3: molar mass as the gram mass of 1 mol (line 61), Example 5.3.4 mass-to-moles with the reciprocal of molar mass (line 122), Example 5.3.1 moles to molecules with 6.022 x 10^23 (line 33); atomic masses from 3.4 Table 3.4.1 (C 12.011 line 60, O 15.999 line 55). Arithmetic: 50.0/44.009 = 1.13613; x 6.022e23 = 6.842e23.

q: What mass of hydrogen gas is produced when 50.0 g of zinc reacts completely with hydrochloric acid? Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) -> ZnCl2(aq) + H2(g)
expect: Mass-mass calculation: mass Zn -> mol Zn -> mol H2 -> mass H2. 50.0 g Zn x (1 mol Zn / 65.39 g Zn) = 0.7646 mol Zn; x (1 mol H2 / 1 mol Zn) = 0.7646 mol H2; x (2.016 g H2 / 1 mol H2) = 1.54 g H2. (Using Table 3.4.1's Zn 65.409 or H2 = 2.02 g/mol also gives 1.54 g.)

Zn molar mass 65.39 g/mol as used in 5.6 Example 5.6.1 (line 37); H from Table 3.4.1 (1.008). Arithmetic: 50.0/65.39 = 0.76464; x 2.016 = 1.5415 -> 1.54 g (x 2.02 = 1.5446 -> 1.54).

q: 10.0 g of rubidium is mixed with 10.0 g of MgCl2 and they react by 2Rb + MgCl2 -> Mg + 2RbCl. Which reactant is limiting, how many grams of Mg form, and how much of the excess reactant is left over?
expect: Compute the Mg from each reactant (Rb 85.47, MgCl2 95.21, Mg 24.31 g/mol). From Rb: 10.0/85.47 = 0.1170 mol Rb x (1 mol Mg/2 mol Rb) x 24.31 = 1.42 g Mg. From MgCl2: 10.0/95.21 = 0.1050 mol x (1/1) x 24.31 = 2.55 g Mg. Rb gives less, so Rb is the limiting reagent and 1.42 g Mg forms. MgCl2 reacted: 0.1170 mol Rb x (1 mol MgCl2/2 mol Rb) x 95.21 = 5.57 g; left over = 10.0 - 5.57 = 4.43 g MgCl2 (remember to subtract; 5.57 g is the amount reacted, not remaining).
note: Same reaction and molar masses as Beginning Chemistry Example 5.7.1 (5.00 g Rb + 3.44 g MgCl2, lines 57-79), with new amounts. Method: whichever reactant gives the lesser amount of product is limiting (line 23); leftover by subtraction (lines 45-53). Arithmetic: 10.0/85.47 = 0.117000; /2 x 24.31 = 1.4222; 10.0/95.21 = 0.105031 x 24.31 = 2.5533; 0.117000/2 x 95.21 = 5.5698; 10.0 - 5.57 = 4.43.

q: For the combustion 2C4H10 + 13O2 -> 8CO2 + 10H2O, how many moles of O2 are needed to burn 6.50 mol of butane, and how many moles of CO2 form?
expect: Mole-mole calculations with ratios from the coefficients (exact numbers, so they don't limit sig figs): O2: 6.50 mol C4H10 x (13 mol O2 / 2 mol C4H10) = 42.25 -> 42.3 mol O2. CO2: 6.50 mol C4H10 x (8 mol CO2 / 2 mol C4H10) = 26.0 mol CO2.
note: Same equation as Beginning Chemistry Example 5.4.2 (154 mol O2 -> 94.8 mol CO2, lines 74-90), now starting from butane. Coefficients are exact numbers (line 90). Arithmetic: 6.50 x 13/2 = 42.25 -> 42.3 (book's rounding rule: first dropped digit 5 rounds up); 6.50 x 8/2 = 26.0.

q: How common is deuterium among hydrogen atoms, and what's the difference between deuterium and tritium?
expect: About one in a million hydrogen atoms is deuterium, which has a proton and a neutron in its nucleus. Tritium is a very rare form of hydrogen with one proton and two neutrons. Both are isotopes of hydrogen (same number of protons, different numbers of neutrons); most hydrogen atoms have just a single proton.
note: Beginning Chemistry 3.2 line 38. 'deuterium' occurs only in 3.2; 'isotope' hits 9 files (heavy in 15-2, 15-3, 15-5), none of which give the deuterium abundance.

q: my teacher crossed out some ions on both sides of an equation and called them spectators. what is a spectator ion and why are you allowed to cancel them?
expect: In a complete ionic equation (dissolved ionic compounds written as separated ions), spectator ions are ions that appear unchanged on both the reactant and product sides; they do nothing in the overall course of the reaction. They are canceled from both sides, like algebraic quantities, leaving the net ionic equation, which shows the actual chemical change. Example: in Na^+ + Cl^- + Ag^+ + NO3^- -> AgCl(s) + Na^+ + NO3^-, Na^+ and NO3^- are spectators and the net ionic equation is Cl^-(aq) + Ag^+(aq) -> AgCl(s). The spectator ions are still present in solution; they just undergo no net change.
note: Defined only in Beginning Chemistry 4.4 (lines 84-96). Grep 'spectator' across both books: 5 files - 04-4 (5), 04-6 (2), 04-7 (1), 07-6 (1), 14-2 (1); orgchem 0. Likely false positives: 04-6 (cancels Na^+/Cl^- in neutralization without defining the term), 04-7 and 14-2 (identical sentence that spectator ions are omitted from a net ionic redox equation), 07-6 (Hess's law analogy 'much like a spectator ion').

q: What is an exact number, and why doesn't the 1000 in a conversion factor like 1000 g / 1 kg limit the significant figures of my answer?
expect: An exact number comes from a defined relationship, not a measurement. The prefix kilo- means exactly 1,000, so in (1000 g / 1 kg) neither the 1000 nor the 1 enters the significant-figure count; they can be thought of as having an infinite number of significant figures. The other (measured) numbers in the calculation determine the significant figures of the result (e.g. the 1 and 100 in cm-to-m factors in Example 2.5.5).
note: Taught in Beginning Chemistry 2.5 (lines 217-225, 237). Grep 'exact number' across both books: 5 files - 02-5 (3), 02-6 (1), 05-4 (1), 15-3 (1), 15-4 (1); orgchem 0. False positives: 15-3 and 15-4 use it in a different sense ('not an exact number of half-lives'); 02-6 (the 1 in a density is exact) and 05-4 (coefficients 8 and 13 are exact) apply the idea without defining it.

q: When a fuel that contains nitrogen burns completely, what happens to the nitrogen? Does it end up as NO2?
expect: No. In a combustion reaction the reactant combines with oxygen to give oxides of all the other elements, but any nitrogen in the reactant is converted to elemental nitrogen, N2, not to a nitrogen-oxygen compound. Examples: 4NH3 + 3O2 -> 2N2 + 6H2O, and for dinitroethylene 2C2H2N2O4 + O2 -> 4CO2 + 2H2O + 2N2.
note: Only Beginning Chemistry 4.5 states the nitrogen rule (lines 55, 69-71, Example 4.5.2b line 89, Key Takeaways line 108). Grep 'combustion' across both books: 5 files - 04-5 (14), 16-2 (5), 07-6 (4), 05-6 (1), 15-6 (1); orgchem 0. Likely false positives: 16-2 (hydrocarbon combustion gives CO2 and H2O, says nothing about N), 07-6 (combustion of C and CO in Hess's law), 05-6 (CO as a side product of methane combustion).

q: How can I predict whether mixing two ionic solutions will give a precipitate?
expect: Treat it as a possible double-replacement reaction: swap the cations (or anions) to get the possible products, then check every compound against the solubility rules. If a product is insoluble it gets the (s) label and precipitates, so a precipitation reaction occurs (the solid forming is the driving force); if everything is soluble, no reaction is expected. Example: Na2SO4(aq) + SrCl2(aq) -> 2NaCl(aq) + SrSO4(s), because sulfates are soluble except with Sr^2+ (and Hg2^2+, Pb^2+, Ba^2+); NaOH + FeCl2 gives Fe(OH)2(s); Ca(NO3)2 + KBr gives no reaction.
note: Taught in Beginning Chemistry 4.3 (lines 141-183, Tables 4.3.1-4.3.2). Grep 'precipitat' across both books: 7 files - 04-3 (9), 04-4 (2), 07-4 (1), 10-5 (1), 11-2 (1), 11-5 (1), 13-6 (1); orgchem 0. 'solubility rules' also hits 04-4, 04-6, 13-6. False positives: 11-2 (precipitation from supersaturated solutions), 07-4 and 11-5 (a precipitation used in a calculation), 13-6 (Ksp / tartrate crystals), 04-4 (net ionic equations for precipitations, not how to predict them). Note: Table 4.3.1 prints sulfate as SO4^2 (missing minus; [Note] line 154), which doesn't change this answer.

q: Should atomic masses be written in u or amu? What exactly is 1 u?
expect: The book uses u for the atomic mass unit; 'amu' is an older style that is no longer accepted. 1 u is defined as one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom (6 protons, 6 neutrons). On this scale a proton is 1.00728 u, a neutron 1.00866 u and an electron 0.000549 u.
note: Beginning Chemistry 3.4 line 20. Token: written 'u' and 'amu' in parentheses: '(u; some texts use amu, but this older style is no longer accepted)'. 'amu' occurs in only this file across both books; other files use u or g/mol without discussing the symbol.

q: In an equation like 2H2(g) + O2(g) -> 2H2O(ℓ), what do the (g), (ℓ), (s) and (aq) labels mean?
expect: They are phase labels: (s) solid, (ℓ) liquid, (g) gas, and (aq) aqueous, i.e. dissolved in water. Special conditions such as temperature may be written above the arrow, e.g. 2NaHCO3(s) -> (200 C) Na2CO3(s) + CO2(g) + H2O(l).
note: Beginning Chemistry 4.2 line 75 lists the labels; 3.6 line 15 explains (aq) ('aq stands for aqueous'). Token: the liquid label is written with the script ell '(ℓ)' in 4.2 (and many equations), though some equations in the corpus use plain '(l)' (e.g. 4.2 line 77, 4.7, 5.7).

q: What's the difference between NO3^- and NO2^-, and which one makes nitric acid versus nitrous acid?
expect: NO3^- is nitrate and NO2^- is nitrite: the -ite ion has one less oxygen atom than the -ate ion but the same charge (1-). For acids, an -ate anion gives an -ic acid and an -ite anion gives an -ous acid, so HNO3 is nitric acid and HNO2 is nitrous acid.
note: Beginning Chemistry 3.5 Table 3.5.2 (line 172-173: 'nitrate | NO3^-', 'nitrite | NO2^-') and line 166 on -ite vs -ate; 3.6 line 19 (-ic/-ous rule), Table 3.6.1 (HNO3 nitric acid, line 30) and Exercise 3.6.1b (HNO2 = nitrous acid, line 64). Tokens written as NO3^− and NO2^− (Unicode minus).

q: When I write 0.000028 in scientific notation, which way do I move the decimal point, and is the power of 10 positive or negative?
expect: Move the decimal point five places to the right to get 2.8, and the power is negative: 2.8 x 10^-5. (Conversely, 56,900 -> 5.69 x 10^4 moves the decimal four places to the left with a positive power.) The power of 10 is positive for numbers greater than 1 and negative for numbers between 0 and 1.
note: Misprint: Beginning Chemistry 2.2 line 90 says the power 'is positive if you move the decimal point to the right and negative if you move the decimal point to the left' (reversed). The [Note] at line 94 corrects it: 0.000028 -> 2.8 moves five places to the right and the power is negative, 10^-5; 56,900 -> 5.69 moves four places left, 10^4. Key Takeaways line 105 agree with the note. A model following line 90 literally would claim a positive exponent. UPDATE: the corpus now corrects this misprint in place, and the [Note: corrected; the source prints … where this reads …] after the paragraph records what the book printed. A correct answer gives the corrected value and doesn't repeat the printed one quoted in the note.

q: Does one mole of ordinary carbon have a mass of exactly 12 grams?
expect: No. Only carbon-12 has a mass of exactly 12 g per mole. Natural carbon is a mixture of isotopes, and its molar mass is 12.011 g/mol (the value used in molar-mass calculations, e.g. 6 C = 6 x 12.011 for C6H12O6).
note: Misprint: Beginning Chemistry 5.3 line 51 says 'by definition, a mole of carbon has a mass of exactly 12 g'. The [Note] at line 55 corrects it: only carbon-12 is exactly 12 g/mol; natural carbon is 12.011 g/mol, as used in Example 5.3.2 (line 74) and Table 3.4.1 (3.4 line 60). Related [Note] at line 21 on the 2019 redefinition of the mole.

q: Does every redox reaction need at least two different elements to change oxidation number?
expect: No. What every redox reaction needs is at least one atom oxidized and one atom reduced, and these can be the same element. In 2H2O2 -> 2H2O + O2, oxygen is both oxidized (-1 to 0, in O2) and reduced (-1 to -2, in H2O) while no other element changes oxidation number.
note: Misprint: Beginning Chemistry 4.7 line 62 says 'At least two elements must change their oxidation numbers.' The [Note] at line 64 corrects this with the H2O2 example. FALSE-POSITIVE RISK: 14.2 (14-2-Oxidation-Reduction-Reactions, line 59) repeats the same sentence with no [Note], so retrieving it alone would give the wrong answer; it is deliberately not in files.

q: why do we have to put temperature in kelvin for charles's law but my teacher lets us use celsius in q = mcΔT?
expect: In gas laws the volume of a gas is proportional to its absolute temperature, not its Celsius temperature, so V/T is constant only when T is in kelvins (K = °C + 273); all gas-law temperatures must be in kelvins. In q = mcΔT only a temperature CHANGE appears, and a change has the same value whether the temperatures are in degrees Celsius or kelvins, so specific heat can be in J/g·°C or J/g·K.
note: Tests linking two sections. 06-4 line 111 ('the volume of a gas is related to its absolute temperature in Kelvin, not its temperature in degrees Celsius'), line 119 ('all temperatures must be expressed in the absolute temperature scale (Kelvin)'), summary line 205. 07-3 line 81 explains the 'departure from the insistence that temperature be expressed in Kelvin' because a change in temperature is the same in °C or K. q: A gas is collected over water in a 3.50 L container at 50°C. The total pressure inside is 833 torr. How many moles of the gas were collected?

q: magnesium's 1st and 2nd ionization energies are 738 and 1450 but the 3rd is like 7700?? why is the third one so huge

q: Why is the lattice energy of MgO (3,791 kJ/mol) so much bigger than that of NaCl (786 kJ/mol)?

MgO is made of Mg2+ and O2- ions (two electrons transferred), with double the charges of Na+ and Cl-, so its lattice energy, the measured strength of ionic bonding, is much larger (Table 9.3.1: MgO 3,791 vs NaCl 786 kJ/mol).

q: CH2Cl2 has a smaller molar mass than CF4, so why does it boil so much higher?

CF4 is nonpolar and has only dispersion forces. So CH2Cl2 boils at 313 K (40°C) while CF4 boils at 145 K (-128°C), even though CH2Cl2's molar mass (85 g/mol) is lower than CF4's (88 g/mol).

q: What causes London dispersion forces, and why are they stronger for bigger molecules?

The more electrons a species has, the stronger the dispersion force (mass is a factor too), which partly explains why small molecules are gases and larger ones are liquids or solids at the same temperature.

q: why does a pot of boiling water stay at 100 degrees even though the stove keeps pumping heat into it?
expect: Because boiling is a phase change, and phase changes are isothermal: during boiling the energy goes exclusively to changing the phase (separating the particles so liquid becomes gas, ΔH_vap), not to changing the temperature. Only when all of the substance has boiled does additional energy go to raising its temperature. The same holds for melting.

q: Why does a salt crystal shatter when you hit it, while a metal just bends or flattens?

Displacing the ions by only about 1 × 10^-10 m puts ions next to ions of the same charge, so they repel, and the crystal breaks; ionic solids are brittle. A metallic solid is held by metallic bonding, the sharing of the s valence electrons by all the atoms, so metals can be hammered into sheets and drawn into wires (and conduct heat and electricity).

q: If you're stuck on a lifeboat in the ocean why can't you just drink the seawater? it's water

(Fresh water is fine from an osmotic standpoint.)

q: why does wax dissolve in hexane but not in water, while table salt does the opposite?
expect: Because of intermolecular interactions: a solute tends to dissolve in a solvent whose molecules experience the same intermolecular forces ('like dissolves like'). NaCl is very polar (made of ions) and dissolves in very polar water but not in nonpolar oil; nonpolar wax dissolves in nonpolar hexane but not in polar water. It is a general rule, not an absolute one.

Example 11.2.2 (I2 in CCl4) supports. 16-2 and 16-4 mention hydrocarbon/alcohol solubility in water but not the general rule.

q: Why would a vat of boiling base be more dangerous than a vat of boiling acid?
expect: Because it is much easier for an OH^- ion (mass 17) to rip an H^+ ion (mass 1) off surrounding matter than for an H^+ ion to rip off an OH^- ion. Concentrated bases (some household cleaners) can immediately remove H^+ ions from flesh, causing chemical burns, whereas we routinely ingest acids (citrus, vinegar, wine); our bodies cope with acids better than bases (though eyes are sensitive to both).

q: how does an acetic acid / sodium acetate buffer keep the pH from changing when you add a strong acid or a strong base?
expect: Each component neutralizes one kind of addition. Added OH^- (strong base) reacts with the weak acid: HC2H3O2 + OH^- -> H2O + C2H3O2^-, so it becomes water instead of making the solution basic. Added H^+ (strong acid) reacts with the acetate ion from the salt: H^+ + C2H3O2^- -> HC2H3O2, forming the weak acid, which does not ionize much. So the pH changes little. This works only up to the buffer's capacity: once either component is used up, the pH can change rapidly.
note: 12-8 lines 17-29 (HC2H3O2/NaC2H3O2 example with both equations, Figure 12.8.1) and line 86 (buffer capacity). The blood HCO3^-/H2CO3 buffer (line 88) is a related example; 11-1 line 27 mentions HCO3^- controlling blood acid-base properties but does not explain buffer action. q: Why is a solution of sodium acetate basic, while a solution of ammonium chloride is acidic and table salt is neutral?
expect: Because of hydrolysis of ions that come from weak acids or bases. Ions from strong acids/bases (Na^+, Cl^-) do not hydrolyze, so NaCl is a neutral salt. The acetate ion comes from a weak acid, so it takes H^+ from water: C2H3O2^- + H2O <-> HC2H3O2 + OH^-, producing OH^- (basic salt). NH4^+ comes from the weak base NH3, so it donates H^+: NH4^+ + H2O <-> NH3 + H3O^+, making the solution acidic (acid salt). Rule: an ion from a weak acid makes the solution basic; an ion from a weak base makes it acidic.
note: 12-5 lines 99-146: NaCl analysis (neutral salt, line 129), 'Thus NaC2H3O2 solutions are slightly basic, so such a salt is called a basic salt' (line 135), NH4Cl as an acid salt (lines 137-141), the two general rules (lines 143-146). 'hydrolysis' (case-insensitive) appears only in 12-3 and 12-5; 12-3 defines hydrolysis with NH3 but does not treat salts.

q: A patient gets a 10.0 mg dose of iodine-131. How much I-131 is left after 20.0 days?

q: why can't you just make an atomic bomb out of natural uranium? isn't uranium radioactive anyway

A bomb needs a chain reaction (each fission releases on average two extra neutrons, which induce more fissions, growing exponentially), and at low U-235 concentrations the chain reaction cannot sustain itself. Uranium must be enriched to about 3% U-235 for reactors and to 70% or more for a bomb; enrichment is laborious and costly.

Amide bonds link amino acids together in proteins.

q: carbon uses a 2s and 2p orbitals to bond, so why are all four C-H bonds in methane the same?

Each overlaps a hydrogen 1s orbital, giving four identical C–H bonds (439 kJ/mol, 109 pm) with 109.5° H–C–H angles. The hybrids are unsymmetrical, with one larger lobe (the + p lobe adds to the s orbital, the − lobe subtracts), so they overlap more effectively and form stronger bonds than unhybridized s or p orbitals.

q: What is the difference between a bonding and an antibonding molecular orbital?
expect: In MO theory atomic orbitals combine into molecular orbitals that belong to the whole molecule. For H2, the additive combination of two 1s orbitals gives a lower-energy bonding MO whose electrons spend most of their time between the nuclei, holding them together; the subtractive combination gives a higher-energy antibonding MO with a node between the nuclei, so its electrons can't contribute to bonding and the nuclei repel. In H2 the bonding MO is filled and the antibonding MO is empty. Likewise in ethylene, combining p lobes of the same sign gives the bonding π MO (no node, filled) and opposite signs give the antibonding π MO (node, vacant).

With four valence electrons it needs four more to reach the neon configuration, so it forms four bonds.

q: Why can phosphorus form five bonds and sulfur four, when nitrogen and oxygen only form three and two?

Beginning Chemistry calls these expanded valence shell molecules: they form only with central atoms in the third row or beyond that have empty d orbitals in their valence shells (e.g. SF6). Second-row nitrogen (5 valence electrons) and oxygen (6) form 3 and 2 bonds to complete an octet.

q: how do valence bond theory and MO theory describe the bond in H2 differently?
expect: Valence bond theory: a covalent bond forms when a singly occupied orbital on one atom overlaps a singly occupied orbital on another; in H2 two 1s orbitals overlap head-on and the paired electrons are attracted to both nuclei, giving a cylindrically symmetric σ bond. MO theory: the two 1s atomic orbitals combine mathematically into molecular orbitals belonging to the whole molecule, a lower-energy egg-shaped bonding MO (holding both electrons) and a higher-energy antibonding MO with a node (empty). The bonding MO is a single orbital, not the same as the two overlapping 1s orbitals of the VB picture. VB theory is easier to visualize, so the book mostly uses it.

q: why does neopentane boil so much lower than pentane if they have the exact same formula?
expect: Increased branching lowers an alkane's boiling point. Pentane (no branches) boils at 36.1 °C, isopentane (2-methylbutane, one branch) at 27.85 °C and neopentane (2,2-dimethylpropane, two branches) at 9.5 °C; likewise octane boils at 125.7 °C but isooctane (2,2,4-trimethylpentane) at 99.3 °C. Alkanes are held together only by weak dispersion forces; branched-chain alkanes are more nearly spherical than straight-chain ones, so they have smaller surface areas and therefore smaller dispersion forces, and less energy is needed to boil them.

q: if a flat hexagon has 120° angles, how come cyclohexane has basically zero ring strain? what did Baeyer get wrong?
expect: Baeyer (1885) assumed all cycloalkanes are flat, so rings whose angles deviate from 109° would suffer angle strain. In fact rings other than cyclopropane and cyclobutane pucker into three-dimensional conformations with nearly tetrahedral angles. Cyclohexane adopts a chair conformation in which all C–C–C angles are 111.5°, close to 109°, and all neighbouring C–H bonds are staggered, so it has neither angle strain nor torsional strain: it is strain-free. Heats of combustion per CH2 confirm this (cyclohexane and rings of 14 or more carbons are strain-free; cyclopropane 115 and cyclobutane about 110 kJ/mol). Ring strain has three contributions: angle strain, torsional strain (eclipsing of neighbouring bonds) and steric strain (nonbonded atoms too close).

The 120° of a planar hexagon is the student's own premise; the book frames it as Baeyer's planar model. Likely false positives: orgchem/04-4-Conformations-of-Cycloalkanes (cyclopropane/cyclobutane/cyclopentane, not cyclohexane), orgchem/04-6-Axial-and-Equatorial-Bonds-in-Cyclohexane, orgchem/03-6-Conformations-of-Ethane (torsional strain only), orgchem/01-8 or other hybridization sections that mention 120° sp2 angles.

q: Using the 1,3-diaxial strain values for monosubstituted cyclohexanes and ΔE = −RT ln K, about what percentage of isopropylcyclohexane molecules have the isopropyl group equatorial at 25 °C?

Table 4.7.1 gives 4.6 kJ/mol of 1,3-diaxial strain for CH(CH3)2 per interaction with one hydrogen; an axial substituent has two such interactions, so the value must be doubled: ΔE = 2 × 4.6 = 9.2 kJ/mol. Then K = e^(ΔE/RT) = e^(9200 / (8.315 × 298)) ≈ 41, so the equatorial fraction is K/(1 + K) ≈ 41/42 ≈ 97.6%, axial ≈ 2.4%. (For comparison, the book's methylcyclohexane, ΔE = 7.6 kJ/mol, is about 95 : 5.)

q: Is water a nucleophile or an electrophile? My notes seem to call it both.
expect: Both, depending on the circumstances. A nucleophile has an electron-rich atom and forms a bond by donating an electron pair to an electron-poor atom; an electrophile has an electron-poor atom and forms a bond by accepting an electron pair from a nucleophile. A neutral compound with an electron-rich site must also have an electron-poor site, so it can often react either way: water acts as a nucleophile when it donates a nonbonding (lone) pair of electrons and as an electrophile when it donates H+. (The book lists water among its example nucleophiles, with ammonia, hydroxide and chloride ion.) Nucleophiles correspond to Lewis bases and electrophiles to Lewis acids.
note: DISTRACTOR: 'nucleophile' appears in 91 corpus files (orgchem chapters 6-30, inorgchem 06-x and 12-x, etc.), but the definitions and the water case are taught in orgchem 06-3: line 65 (definitions; 'ammonia, water, hydroxide ion, and chloride ion are examples'), line 70 ('Water, for instance, acts as an electrophile when it donates H^+ but acts as a nucleophile when it donates a nonbonding pair of electrons'), line 72 (Lewis base = nucleophile, Lewis acid = electrophile). Likely false positives: inorgchem/06-4-Lewis-Concept-and-Frontier-Orbitals (line 78 onward defines nucleophile/electrophile as fast-reacting Lewis bases/acids but never discusses water's dual role), inorgchem/06-1-Acid-Base-Models-as-Organizing-Concepts (one-line table entry), orgchem/06-5-Using-Curved-Arrows-in-Polar-Reaction-Mechanisms (charge bookkeeping for nucleophiles), orgchem/11-3-Characteristics-of-the-SN2-Reaction (nucleophilicity), orgchem/06-13-Key-Terms (term list only).

q: If a reaction breaks reactant bonds with a total strength of 380 kJ/mol and forms product bonds with a total strength of 400 kJ/mol, what is ΔH and is the reaction exothermic or endothermic?
expect: ΔH = (strength of bonds broken) − (strength of bonds formed) = 380 kJ/mol − 400 kJ/mol = −20 kJ/mol. ΔH is negative, so the reaction is exothermic: the products have stronger bonds and are more stable than the reactants, and heat is released.
