q: whats the difference between a transition state and an intermediate on a reaction energy diagram? they both look like the stuff in the middle
expect: A transition state is the highest-energy structure of a step, sitting at an energy maximum (the top of the barrier); it is an activated complex with bonds partially broken and partially formed (for HBr + ethylene, the C=C π bond and H–Br bond partly broken and the C–H bond partly formed), it is unstable and can't be isolated, and its height above the reactants is the activation energy ΔG‡. An intermediate (such as the carbocation in HBr + ethylene) is a species formed in one step and consumed in a later step of a multistep reaction; it lies in an energy minimum between two transition states, so it is more stable than its neighbouring transition states, but it is higher in energy than the reactant that formed it and the product it gives, so it normally can't be isolated. Each step has its own transition state, ΔG‡ and ΔG°; the overall rate is set by the energy difference between the reactants and the highest transition state.
note: 06-9 lines 21-23 ('a structure of maximum energy is reached, a structure called the transition state ... It is unstable and can't be isolated ... activated complex ... partially broken ... partially formed') and line 28 (activation energy ΔG‡). 06-10 line 14 (carbocation 'exists only transiently ... a reaction intermediate'), line 16 ('the reaction intermediate lies at an energy minimum between steps ... can't normally be isolated. It is, however, more stable than its two neighboring transition states'), line 21 (overall ΔG‡ to the highest transition state). inorgchem 12-1 lines 70-72 give the same contrast in a glossary ('a transition state is the transient species that exists at an energy maximum'; 'an intermediate is a high-energy structure at a local minimum ... sometimes exist long enough and in high enough concentration to be detectable experimentally'). Likely false positives: physchem/28-8-Transition-State-Theory-Can-Be-Used-to-Estimate-Reaction-Rate-Constants (TST rate constants, no intermediate), orgchem/07-10-The-Hammond-Postulate (transition-state structure resembles nearest species), orgchem/07-9-Carbocation-Structure-and-Stability, physchem/29-8-A-Catalyst-Affects-the-Mechanism-and-Activation-Energy.

q: What alcohol do you get from hydroboration–oxidation of 1-methylcyclopentene, and what are the regiochemistry and stereochemistry of the addition?
expect: trans-2-Methylcyclopentanol (85% yield). Borane (BH3, as the BH3–THF complex) adds its B–H bond across the C=C, and the organoborane is then oxidized with basic hydrogen peroxide (H2O2, OH−), which replaces boron with –OH with the same stereochemistry. The H and B add from the same face (syn addition) with boron on the less highly substituted carbon, so the overall result is syn, non-Markovnikov addition of water: the OH ends up on the less substituted carbon, trans to the methyl group. The reaction occurs in a single step with no carbocation intermediate (C–H and C–B bonds form at the same time on the same face), and boron goes to the less sterically crowded carbon. This is complementary to oxymercuration–demercuration, which gives the Markovnikov alcohol.
note: 08-5 line 10 (BH3, organoborane RBH2, oxidation with basic H2O2), line 14 (BH3–THF complex), line 22 ('hydroboration–oxidation of 1-methylcyclopentene yields trans-2-methylcyclopentanol ... syn stereochemistry ... boron attaching to the less highly substituted carbon ... overall syn non-Markovnikov addition of water'), line 24 image (85 percent yield), line 26 (single step, no carbocation, steric reason). 08-16 line 16 summarizes both hydration methods as complementary. Existing q124 covers Markovnikov HBr addition; this one is the non-Markovnikov counterpart. Likely false positives: orgchem/08-4-Hydration-of-Alkenes-Addition-of-H2O-by-Oxymercuration (Markovnikov hydration), orgchem/09-4-Hydration-of-Alkynes (hydroboration of alkynes gives aldehydes), orgchem/17-3-Preparation-of-Alcohols-A-Review, inorgchem/13-1-Introduction-to-Organometallic-Chemistry (mentions hydroboration in passing).

q: What does ozonolysis do to an alkene, and why is the ozonide treated with zinc afterwards?
expect: Ozone (O3, made by passing O2 through a high-voltage electrical discharge) adds rapidly to the C=C bond at low temperature to give a cyclic molozonide, which spontaneously rearranges to an ozonide. Low-molecular-weight ozonides are explosive, so they are not isolated but immediately treated with a reducing agent such as zinc metal in acetic acid, which gives carbonyl compounds. Net result: the C=C bond is cleaved and each of the original alkene carbons becomes doubly bonded to an oxygen. A tetrasubstituted alkene gives two ketones and a trisubstituted alkene gives one ketone and one aldehyde; e.g. isopropylidenecyclohexane gives cyclohexanone and acetone.
note: 08-8 line 12 (ozone preparation, molozonide, ozonide), line 16 ('Low-molecular-weight ozonides are explosive and therefore not isolated ... zinc metal in acetic acid ... the C=C bond is cleaved and an oxygen atom becomes doubly bonded to each of the original alkene carbons'; tetrasubstituted -> two ketones, trisubstituted -> ketone + aldehyde), line 18 image (isopropylidenecyclohexane -> cyclohexanone + acetone). Likely false positives: orgchem/08-17-Summary-of-Reactions (reaction scheme only, lines 80-84), orgchem/09-6-Oxidative-Cleavage-of-Alkynes (O3/KMnO4 on alkynes gives carboxylic acids), orgchem/19-2-Preparing-Aldehydes-and-Ketones (O3/Zn as a route to ketones in an exercise), inorgchem/08-11-The-Oxygen-Family-The-Chalcogens (line 418: ozonolysis locates double bonds, no mechanism), orgchem/08-7 (KMnO4/OsO4 hydroxylation, not cleavage).

q: how do i turn an alkyne into a trans alkene? hydrogenating with Lindlar's catalyst keeps giving me the cis one
expect: Use sodium or lithium metal in liquid ammonia instead; this dissolving-metal reduction is complementary to the Lindlar reduction and gives trans alkenes (e.g. 5-decyne -> trans-5-decene, 78%). Lindlar hydrogenation (H2 over Pd on CaCO3 deactivated with lead acetate and quinoline) adds H2 with syn stereochemistry, so it stops at the cis alkene; H2 over Pd/C reduces all the way to the alkane. In Li/NH3 (a deep blue solution of solvated electrons at −33 °C), an electron adds to the triple bond to give an anion radical, which takes H+ from NH3 to give a vinylic radical; a second electron gives a vinylic anion, which is protonated. The trans geometry is set when the vinylic radical is reduced: vinylic radicals equilibrate rapidly between cis and trans, but the less hindered, more stable trans vinylic anion forms and is protonated before it can equilibrate.
note: 09-5 line 14 (Pd/C -> alkane; Lindlar catalyst composition; 'syn stereochemistry ..., giving a cis alkene'), line 22 ('sodium or lithium metal ... in liquid ammonia ... produces trans rather than cis alkenes. For example, 5-decyne gives trans-5-decene'), line 24 image (78%), line 26 (mechanism: anion radical, vinylic radical, vinylic anion), line 31 (why trans). 09-12 line 16 summarizes: Lindlar -> cis alkene, Li/NH3 -> trans alkene. Likely false positives: orgchem/08-6-Reduction-of-Alkenes-Hydrogenation (syn hydrogenation of alkenes), orgchem/07-4-Cis-Trans-Isomerism-in-Alkenes (cis/trans definitions; existing q116), orgchem/09-9-An-Introduction-to-Organic-Synthesis and 09-8 (mention Lindlar in synthesis problems), orgchem/09-11-Key-Terms.

q: Using the relative reactivities of primary and secondary hydrogens toward radical chlorination, what percentages of 1-chloropropane and 2-chloropropane would you expect from monochlorination of propane?
expect: About 46% 1-chloropropane and 54% 2-chloropropane. Toward chlorination a secondary hydrogen is about 3.5 times as reactive as a primary one (and a tertiary about 5 times). Propane has six primary hydrogens (two CH3 groups) and two secondary hydrogens (the CH2): relative amounts 6 × 1 = 6 for 1-chloropropane and 2 × 3.5 = 7 for 2-chloropropane, so 6/13 = 46% and 7/13 = 54%. The book derives the 3.5 factor from butane (30 : 70 for 1- and 2-chlorobutane: 30% ÷ 6 = 5% per primary H, 70% ÷ 4 = 17.5% per secondary H, 17.5 ÷ 5 = 3.5). The order follows C–H bond strengths: primary 421, secondary 410, tertiary 400 kJ/mol.

q: why does HBr + 1,3-butadiene give mostly the 1,2 product in the cold but mostly the 1,4 product when it's warmer?
expect: Kinetic versus thermodynamic control. At 0 °C the addition gives a 71 : 29 mixture of 1,2 and 1,4 adducts; at 40 °C it gives 15 : 85, and heating the 0 °C mixture to 40 °C with HBr slowly changes 71 : 29 to 15 : 85. At low temperature the additions are irreversible, so the product ratio depends only on relative rates: the 1,2 adduct forms faster (lower ΔG‡) and predominates (kinetic control). At higher temperature the additions become readily reversible and an equilibrium is reached, so the ratio depends only on stability: the 1,4 adduct is more stable and predominates (thermodynamic, or equilibrium, control). Both adducts come from the same resonance-stabilized allylic carbocation.
note: 14-3 line 10 (71 : 29 at 0 °C, 15 : 85 at 40 °C; mixture equilibrates on heating), line 23 ('The product of an irreversible reaction depends only on relative rates ... kinetic control'), line 27 ('depends only on stability ... equilibrium control, or thermodynamic control'), line 31 (applies it to butadiene). 14-12 line 14 summarizes (1,2 = kinetic, 1,4 = thermodynamic; same allylic carbocation). Grep 'kinetic control|thermodynamic control' over all books: only 14-3, 14-11, 14-12 teach it (orgchem/19-13 and inorgchem 08-2/12-7/14-2 use the terms in passing). Likely false positives: orgchem/14-2-Electrophilic-Additions-to-Conjugated-Dienes-Allylic-Carbocations (1,2 vs 1,4 addition and the allylic cation, not the temperature effect), orgchem/07-8 (Markovnikov; existing q124), orgchem/06-7-Describing-a-Reaction-Equilibria-Rates-and-Energy-Changes (rates vs equilibria in general), introductory/13-4-Shifting-Equilibria-Le-Chateliers-Principle.

q: In UV spectroscopy, what does π → π* mean, and at what wavelength does 1,3-butadiene absorb?
expect: π → π* ('pi to pi star') is the electronic excitation caused by UV absorption in a conjugated molecule: an electron is promoted from a bonding π molecular orbital, the highest occupied MO (HOMO), to an antibonding π* molecular orbital, the lowest unoccupied MO (LUMO). For 1,3-butadiene the electron goes from ψ2 (HOMO) to ψ3* (LUMO), and the HOMO–LUMO gap corresponds to UV light of 217 nm (λmax = 217 nm). The gap shrinks as conjugation increases, so λmax rises (1,3,5-hexatriene 258 nm, 1,3,5,7-octatetraene 290 nm). Instrumental Analysis lists π → π* transitions at roughly 200–500 nm (C=C, C=O, C=N, C≡C), alongside n → π*.

q: When benzaldehyde is nitrated, what percentages of ortho, meta and para nitro products form, and why is meta favoured?
expect: 19% ortho, 72% meta and 9% para (Table 16.1). The –CHO group is a deactivating meta director. Of the three possible carbocation intermediates, the meta intermediate has three favourable resonance forms, while the ortho and para intermediates have only two: their third form puts the positive charge directly on the ring carbon bearing the aldehyde group, where it is disfavoured by repulsion with the positively polarized C=O carbon. So the meta intermediate is more stable and forms faster. In general, a substituent with a positively polarized (δ+) atom attached directly to the ring acts as a meta director.

Table 16.1 above gives 19% ortho, 72% meta and 9% para for the nitration of benzaldehyde (–CHO).] A correct answer gives 19% ortho (which also makes the three figures add to 100: 19 + 72 + 9 = 100), not the printed 1%. q: What are the limitations of Friedel–Crafts alkylation?
expect: Four limitations: (1) only alkyl halides work; aryl and vinylic halides don't react, because aryl and vinylic carbocations are too high in energy to form under Friedel–Crafts conditions. (2) The reaction fails on aromatic rings bearing a strongly electron-withdrawing group (such as a carbonyl) or a basic amino group that can be protonated (the ring must be at least as reactive as a halobenzene). (3) Polyalkylation: once one alkyl group is on the ring a second substitution is easier, so it is hard to stop at one (benzene with 1 equivalent of 2-chloro-2-methylpropane gives mainly p-di-tert-butylbenzene); a large excess of benzene is needed for monoalkylation. (4) The carbocation electrophile can rearrange by hydride or alkyl shift, especially with primary alkyl halides (1-chlorobutane at 0 °C gives about 2 : 1 sec-butyl to butyl product). Friedel–Crafts acylation (RCOCl/AlCl3) shares the substrate limitation but its acyl cation doesn't rearrange and it never occurs more than once.
note: 16-3 line 15 (aryl/vinylic halides don't react), line 19 and Figure 16.3.2 (electron-withdrawing or basic amino substituents), line 24 (polyalkylation, p-di-tert-butylbenzene, excess benzene), line 28 (rearrangement, 2 : 1 sec-butyl : butyl), line 30 (hydride/alkyl shifts), lines 38 and 43 (acylation: same substrate limits, no rearrangement, no multiple acylation). 16-13 line 16 summarizes ('the aromatic ring must be at least as reactive as a halobenzene. In addition, polyalkylation and carbocation rearrangements often occur'). q: What does the D in [α]D stand for, and what units do the pathlength and concentration have to be in when you calculate a specific rotation?
expect: [α]D is the specific rotation: the observed rotation measured with light of 589.6 nm, the sodium D line (the yellow light of sodium street lamps), which is what the subscript D denotes, with pathlength l in decimeters (1 dm = 10 cm) and concentration c in g/cm^3 (g/mL): [α]D = α / (l × c). Units are deg·cm²/g but are usually omitted. Example: cocaine, [α]D = −16, 1.20 g in 7.50 mL (c = 0.160 g/cm^3) in a 5.00 cm tube (l = 0.500 dm) gives α = (−16)(0.500)(0.160) = −1.3°. Enantiomers have equal and opposite values ((+)-lactic acid +3.82, (−)-lactic acid −3.82); + is dextrorotatory (clockwise), − levorotatory.

q: What is the degree of unsaturation of a compound with the formula C9H11NO2?
expect: 5. Ignore the oxygens and subtract the one nitrogen from the hydrogens: C9H11NO2 is equivalent to the hydrocarbon C9H10. The saturated C9 alkane is C9H20 (CnH2n+2), so C9H10 has 20 − 10 = 10 fewer hydrogens = 5 pairs of H2, i.e. five rings and/or multiple bonds (for example a benzene ring, which counts as 4, plus one C=O). Rules: add halogens to the H count, ignore oxygen, subtract nitrogens; each ring or double bond removes two hydrogens from CnH2n+2 (a triple bond counts as 2).
note: Changed-numbers version of 07-2's examples (C6H10 -> 2; C4H6Br2 -> 1; C5H8O -> 2; C5H9N -> 2) and Exercise 7.2.2 (which uses C6H5NO2 and C10H12N2O3, not C9H11NO2). 07-2 line 14 (each ring or double bond = loss of two H), line 16 (C6H10 worked example), lines 22-38 (halogen, oxygen, nitrogen rules; summary list at lines 36-38). Recomputed: H_equiv = 11 − 1 = 10; (2 × 9 + 2 − 10)/2 = (20 − 10)/2 = 5. Forgetting the nitrogen correction gives 4.5 (not an integer); adding instead of subtracting N gives 4. Likely false positives: orgchem/13-12-DEPT-13C-NMR-Spectroscopy and orgchem/13-6-Spin-Spin-Splitting-in-1H-NMR-Spectra (both say to calculate the degree of unsaturation first, citing Section 7.2, without the rules), orgchem/07-13-Key-Terms, introductory/16-2-Hydrocarbons (saturated/unsaturated, existing q243).

q: Does the acetate ion flip back and forth between its two resonance structures? And why are both of its C–O bonds the same length?
expect: No. Resonance forms are imaginary; acetate has a single, unchanging structure, a resonance hybrid of the two forms, with characteristics of both. It doesn't spend part of its time as one form and part as the other; the problem is only that a single line-bond structure can't represent it. The two forms differ only in where the π and nonbonding electrons are drawn; the atoms, their connections, geometry and hybridization (sp2 carbon) are identical. Because the real structure is intermediate between the two forms, the two oxygens are equivalent and share the negative charge equally, and both C–O bonds are 127 pm long, midway between a typical C–O single bond (135 pm) and C=O double bond (120 pm).
note: DISTRACTOR: 'resonance' appears in 123 corpus files (NMR 'magnetic resonance' throughout orgchem 13, analchem 19 and physchem 14; resonance-stabilized cations/anions across orgchem), but resonance forms are taught in orgchem 02-4/02-5. 02-4 line 14 (both C–O bonds 127 pm, 'midway between ... C–O single bond (135 pm) and ... C=O double bond (120 pm)'; both oxygens share the charge), line 18 (only π and nonbonding electrons differ), line 20 ('Acetate doesn't jump back and forth between two resonance forms ... a resonance hybrid'); 02-5 line 14 (Rule 1: forms are imaginary; 'they don't switch back and forth'), line 18 (Rule 2: positions and hybridization unchanged). Likely false positives: inorgchem/03-1-Lewis-Electron-Dot-Diagrams (section 3.1.1 teaches resonance with ozone and carbonate, 'the actual structure is the average', but not acetate or its bond lengths), orgchem/02-10-Organic-Acids-and-Organic-Bases (acetate resonance stabilizes the anion, explaining acidity), orgchem/02-6-Drawing-Resonance-Forms (curved-arrow patterns), orgchem/15-2-Structure-and-Stability-of-Benzene, orgchem/13-x NMR sections (wrong sense of 'resonance').

q: What is the pKa of water? My orgo table says 15.7 but my other notes say 14.
expect: The corpus gives both values. OpenStax Organic Chemistry Table 17.2.1 (acidity of alcohols and phenols) lists H2O at pKa 15.74, between methanol (15.54) and ethanol (16), and Exercise 9.7.1 uses 'pKa of H2O = 15.7'. But the same book's Table 2.8.1 and Worked Example 2.9.1 give water pKa = 14.00, which Section 2.8 derives from H2O + H2O ⇌ H3O+ + OH-, Kw = Ka = [H3O+][OH-] = 1.0 x 10^-14, with water left out of the expression because as the solvent its activity is 1. Inorganic Chemistry Table 6.2.1 also lists water Ka 1.0 x 10^-14, pKa 14.00, and Section 12.9 says 'the pKa for dissociation of a proton from water is pKa = 14'. q: How does a breathalyzer test for alcohol, and what blood alcohol level is illegal for driving?
expect: All 50 US states make it illegal to drive with a blood alcohol concentration (BAC) above 0.08%. The original breath analyzer measured alcohol in expired air by the color change when bright-orange potassium dichromate (K2Cr2O7), the oxidizing agent, is reduced to blue-green chromium(III); current consumer devices use a conductivity sensor, and law-enforcement tests use IR spectroscopy on the expired air. Instrumental Analysis 14.4 describes the dichromate method quantitatively: a 52.5-mL breath sample is bubbled through acidified K2Cr2O7, which oxidizes ethanol to acetic acid, and ethanol is measured by the decrease in dichromate's absorbance at 440 nm; a BAC of 0.10% (above the legal limit) corresponds to 0.025 mg of ethanol in the sample. Context from 17.12: 0.1-0.3% BAC impairs motor coordination, 0.3-0.4% brings nausea and loss of consciousness, above 0.6% can be fatal.

q: What do the numbers in 18-crown-6 mean, and which metal ion does it bind?
expect: Crown ethers are named x-crown-y, where x is the total number of atoms in the ring and y is the number of oxygen atoms, so 18-crown-6 is an 18-membered ring containing 6 ether oxygens (Inorganic Chemistry adds: 6 O and 12 C, joined by -CH2CH2- units). 18-Crown-6 binds potassium ion (K+) strongly in its cavity, so a solution of it in a nonpolar solvent dissolves potassium salts: KMnO4 dissolves in toluene in the presence of 18-crown-6, giving a useful reagent for oxidizing alkenes. Because the cation is strongly solvated and the anion left bare, SN2 reactivity of the anion is greatly enhanced. Smaller crowns bind smaller ions (15-crown-5 Na+; 12-crown-4 Li+ in Organic Chemistry, 14-crown-4 for Li+ in Inorganic Chemistry's table).

Thus, 18-crown-6 ether is an 18-membered ring containing 6 ether oxygen atoms'; line 14 (binds K+, KMnO4 in toluene); line 16 (bare anion, SN2); line 24 (15-crown-5 Na+, 12-crown-4 Li+). inorgchem 08-3 line 188 (18-crown-6 prefers K+; 14-crown-4 Li+, 15-crown-5 Na+, 21-crown-7 Cs+) and footnote line 229 ('the ring of 18-crown-six contains a total of 18 atoms, 6 O and 12 C'). q: Why are aldehydes more reactive than ketones toward nucleophilic addition, and is benzaldehyde more or less reactive than an ordinary aliphatic aldehyde?
expect: For both steric and electronic reasons. Sterically, an aldehyde has only one relatively large substituent on the carbonyl carbon and a ketone two, so the nucleophile's approach (along the C=O at about 75° to the plane of the sp2 orbitals, ~105° from the oxygen) is less hindered for an aldehyde. Electronically, the aldehyde carbonyl is more polarized: like a primary vs a secondary carbocation, an aldehyde has only one alkyl group inductively stabilizing the partial positive charge on the carbonyl carbon, so it is more electrophilic. Aromatic aldehydes such as benzaldehyde are less reactive than aliphatic aldehydes, because the electron-donating resonance effect of the ring makes the carbonyl carbon less positive (less blue in the electrostatic potential map than formaldehyde).

q: What is a nucleophilic acyl substitution, how is it different from an SN2 reaction, and which carboxylic acid derivatives react fastest?
expect: When a nucleophile adds to the C=O of a carboxylic acid derivative, it forms a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate (as with aldehydes and ketones), but because the acyl carbon carries a group -Y that can leave, often as a stable anion, the intermediate expels -Y and re-forms a C=O: the net result is substitution of the nucleophile for -Y. Aldehydes and ketones have no such leaving group, so they give addition instead. It looks like an SN2 substitution, but SN2 is one step with backside displacement, while nucleophilic acyl substitution takes two steps (addition, then elimination) through a tetrahedral intermediate; the addition is usually rate-limiting. Reactivity increases from amide < ester < thioester < acid anhydride < acid chloride: acid chlorides are most reactive because chlorine withdraws electrons from the carbonyl carbon, amides least because nitrogen donates by resonance; unhindered carbonyls react faster than hindered ones. A more reactive derivative can be converted into a less reactive one but not the reverse, and only acyl phosphates, thioesters, esters and amides are common in nature because acid halides and anhydrides hydrolyze too fast.
note: DISTRACTOR: 'nucleophilic acyl substitution' (case-insensitive) occurs in 42 files, all in orgchem: 21-2 x13, 21-3 x12, 18-14 x8, 21-4 x7, 21-8 x6, 29-5 x5, 21-0 x5, and 35 more with 1-4 mentions each (chapter 29 metabolism, 22-8 barbiturates, 26-7 peptide synthesis, 27-5 terpenoids, 24-6 amine synthesis ...), which use the term without teaching it. 21-2 teaches it: line 10 (tetrahedral intermediate eliminates a substituent), line 15 (leaving group -Y; aldehydes/ketones have none), line 19 (vs SN2: one step vs two steps), line 33 (addition rate-limiting), lines 35-45 (steric order; acid chlorides most, amides least reactive; Figure 21.2.2 order amide < ester < thioester < acid anhydride < acid chloride, line 48; acyl phosphates; conversions only downhill; which occur in nature). 18-14 lines 83-87 give the basic definition (Chapter 21 preview). q: How acidic are the alpha hydrogens of acetone, and why do chemists use LDA instead of sodium ethoxide to make an enolate?
expect: Acetone's alpha hydrogens have pKa = 19.3, about 10^40 times more acidic than ethane (pKa ≈ 60), because the enolate's negative charge is shared with the carbonyl oxygen by resonance. But acetone is a weaker acid than ethanol (pKa 16), so sodium ethoxide deprotonates it only to about 0.1%. Lithium diisopropylamide, LDA [LiN(i-C3H7)2], is the lithium salt of diisopropylamine (pKa 36), so it is strong enough to convert most carbonyl compounds completely into their enolates; it is made from butyllithium and diisopropylamine and is soluble in organic solvents (e.g. THF) because of its two alkyl groups. (Table 22.5.1: ketone ~19, aldehyde ~17, ester ~25, 1,3-diketone ~9.)

q: whats the actual difference between a claisen condensation and an aldol? and why does the claisen need a whole equivalent of base instead of just a catalytic amount
expect: Both start the same way: base removes an alpha hydrogen to form an enolate, which adds to the carbonyl group of a second molecule to give a tetrahedral intermediate. The difference is what that intermediate does. In the aldol reaction (aldehydes/ketones) it is protonated to give an alcohol, a beta-hydroxy carbonyl compound, as in nucleophilic addition. In the Claisen condensation (esters) it expels an alkoxide leaving group, a nucleophilic acyl substitution, giving a beta-keto ester; e.g. ethyl acetate with sodium ethoxide gives ethyl acetoacetate (75%). The beta-keto ester product has a highly acidic, doubly activated hydrogen between the two carbonyls, which the base removes; that deprotonation consumes a full equivalent of base and drives the reversible equilibrium completely to the product side, which is why Claisen yields are usually high (acid workup then reprotonates the product).

q: Methylamine is a base, so why does my amine table list its pK_a as 10.64? What is its pK_b?

q: Using the specific rotations the textbook gives for pure alpha- and beta-D-glucopyranose and for the mutarotation equilibrium, work out the alpha:beta ratio at equilibrium. Then, if a freshly dissolved alpha-D-glucopyranose solution has fallen to +80.0 partway through mutarotation, what percent is still the alpha anomer?

Treating the solution as a mixture of the two anomers with mole fraction x of alpha: 112.2x + 18.7(1 - x) = 52.6, so x = (52.6 - 18.7)/(112.2 - 18.7) = 33.9/93.5 = 0.363, i.e. about 36% alpha : 64% beta, matching the book's 37 : 63 equilibrium mixture. At +80.0: x = (80.0 - 18.7)/93.5 = 61.3/93.5 = 0.656, so about 66% is still alpha (34% beta). Mutarotation is the slow interconversion of the anomers by ring-opening to the open-chain aldehyde and reclosure, catalyzed by acid and base.

q: butter and olive oil are both fats right? so why is butter solid at room temp and olive oil liquid? and how do they turn oil into margarine
expect: Both are triacylglycerols (triglycerides), triesters of glycerol with three long-chain fatty acids. The difference is the fatty acids: vegetable oils have a higher proportion of unsaturated fatty acids than animal fats (olive oil is about 80% oleic acid; butter has about 25% palmitic, 10% stearic and 10% myristic acid, and only 25% oleic). Saturated chains have a uniform shape that packs efficiently in a crystal lattice, but the cis (Z) C=C bonds in unsaturated chains introduce bends and kinks that make crystallization harder; the more double bonds, the lower the melting point (stearic acid, C18 saturated, melts at 68.8 °C; oleic acid, C18 with one cis double bond, at 13.4 °C; linoleic at -12 °C). Margarine and shortening were made by catalytic hydrogenation of the C=C bonds (H2 with a nickel catalyst at high temperature) to give saturated solid or semisolid fats; the reaction also isomerizes some remaining double bonds, giving fats with about 10-15% trans fatty acids, which the FDA no longer considers safe (since 2015).
note: Casual phrasing. 27-1 line 14 (fats solid, oils liquid; both triacylglycerols), line 18 (cis geometry), Table 27.1.1 lines 25-35 (melting points), Table 27.1.2 lines 44 and 50 (butter, olive oil compositions), line 59 ('the C═C bonds introduce bends and kinks into the hydrocarbon chains, making crystal formation more difficult'), line 61 (hydrogenation, nickel, 10-15% trans, FDA 2015). 08-6 line 40 (hydrogenation of vegetable oils for margarine; Figure 8.6.2 trans fats). q: What HDL cholesterol level is considered normal for a woman? Is it better for HDL to be high or low?
expect: Higher is better for HDL. Normal values are above 40 mg/dL for men and above 50 mg/dL for women (Table 27.8.1 gives HDL >60 mg/dL as optimal and <40 mg/dL as poor), perhaps explaining why premenopausal women seem somewhat less susceptible to heart disease. HDLs remove cholesterol (as its stearate ester) from dying cells and carry it to the liver, so a high HDL level means more cholesterol is being removed; as a rule of thumb, risk drops about 25% for each 5 mg/dL increase in HDL. LDL, which delivers cholesterol to peripheral tissues, is better low (optimal <100, poor >130 mg/dL). The '<50 mg/dL for women' printed in the book is a misprint.

q: Roughly what percentage of each base is in human DNA, and how many hydrogen bonds hold together a G-C pair compared with an A-T pair?
expect: Human DNA contains about 30% each of adenine and thymine and about 20% each of guanine and cytosine (the bacterium Clostridium perfringens has about 37% A and T, 13% G and C). A always equals T and G equals C because the two complementary strands of the double helix are held together by hydrogen bonds between specific base pairs, A with T and C with G. The G-C pair is held by three hydrogen bonds and the A-T pair by two. (The helix is 20 Å wide, with 10 base pairs and 34 Å per turn, a 12 Å major groove and a 6 Å minor groove.)

q: How many acetyl CoA molecules and how many passes through beta-oxidation do you get from stearic acid (C18)? What about a 17-carbon fatty acid?
expect: Each passage of the four-step beta-oxidation pathway cleaves one two-carbon acetyl group (as acetyl CoA) from the chain, and the final passage on a four-carbon (butyryl) CoA gives two acetyl CoA. Stearic acid, C18: 18/2 = 9 acetyl CoA from 9 - 1 = 8 passages (compare the book's myristic acid, C14: 7 acetyl CoA after 6 passages; palmitic, C16: 8 and 7). A fatty acid with an odd number of carbons gives three-carbon propionyl CoA in the final passage, so C17: (17 - 3)/2 = 7 acetyl CoA plus 1 propionyl CoA, from 7 passages. The propionyl CoA is converted to succinate by a multistep radical pathway, and succinate enters the citric acid cycle.

q: how do i tell if an electrocyclic ring closure goes conrotatory or disrotatory? and does it change if you use light instead of heat
expect: The stereochemistry is set by the symmetry of the polyene's HOMO (frontier orbital theory): the terminal p lobes must rotate so that like-signed lobes overlap. If like lobes are on the same side, they rotate in opposite directions (disrotatory); if on opposite sides, in the same direction (conrotatory). For thermal reactions the ground-state HOMO is used: a conjugated triene (odd number, 3 electron pairs) closes disrotatory, e.g. (2E,4Z,6E)-2,4,6-octatriene gives cis-5,6-dimethyl-1,3-cyclohexadiene; a diene (even, 2 pairs) reacts conrotatory, seen as cyclobutene ring-opening (cis-3,4-dimethylcyclobutene gives (2E,4Z)-2,4-hexadiene). Rule: even number of electron pairs, thermal = conrotatory; odd = disrotatory. Light excites an electron from HOMO to LUMO, changing the frontier orbital's symmetry, so photochemical reactions always go the opposite way: even = disrotatory, odd = conrotatory ((2E,4E)-2,4-hexadiene cyclizes disrotatory with light; (2E,4Z,6E)-octatriene conrotatory to trans-5,6-dimethyl-1,3-cyclohexadiene). Mnemonic (30.9): The Electrons Circle Around - Thermal + Even = Conrotatory.
note: Casual phrasing. 30-2 lines 30-34 (definitions of disrotatory/conrotatory from lobe signs). 30-3 line 10 (HOMO symmetry; ground state for thermal), line 12 (triene disrotatory, octatriene examples), line 19 (diene conrotatory, cyclobutene openings), line 30 ('Polyenes with an even number of electron pairs undergo thermal electrocyclic reactions in a conrotatory sense, whereas polyenes with an odd number ... disrotatory'). 30-4 line 10 (excitation changes symmetry; examples), line 15 and Table 30.4.1 lines 19-22. 30-9 line 16 (TECA) also answers and may be cited. Likely false positives: 30-5/30-6 (cycloadditions, supra/antarafacial), 30-7/30-8 (sigmatropic), 30-10 (vitamin D photochemical ring-opening, example only), 30-12-Summary.

q: What's the difference between high-density and low-density polyethylene, and how is each made?
expect: Low-density polyethylene is the branched product of radical-induced chain-growth polymerization of ethylene. High-density polyethylene is the linear polymer made with a Ziegler-Natta catalyst (an organometallic titanium complex made from an alkylaluminum and a titanium compound, typically (CH3CH2)3Al + TiCl4), which gives chains with practically no branching: 4000 to 7000 ethylene units per chain, molecular weight 100,000 to 200,000 amu. Because the linear chains pack closely and regularly, HDPE is highly crystalline with strong van der Waals forces between chains, so it has greater strength and heat resistance than LDPE; it is used for plastic squeeze bottles and molded housewares (recycling code 2 - HDPE, bottles), while LDPE is code 4 (grocery bags). Higher-molecular-weight grades (HMW, UHMW) are made for pipes, containers, bearings and bulletproof vests. Inorganic Chemistry 14.4 adds that HDPE is a linear homopolymer used for garbage containers, detergent bottles and water pipes, and that linear low-density polyethylene (LLDPE), also made by Ziegler-Natta catalysis, has many short branches.
note: DISTRACTOR: 'polyethylene' appears in 16 files across four books (analchem IR sample cards 17-1 and 07-4, analchem 27-3 'polyethylene glycol' GC phases, inorgchem 08-7 and 13-1, introductory 16-7 addition polymers, orgchem 07-1, 08-0, 08-10, 08-16, 21-9, 31-0, 31-2, 31-7, 31-8, inorgchem 14-4), but only 31-2 explains HDPE vs LDPE: line 21 (linear, no branching), line 17-19 (Et3Al + TiCl4), line 27 ('The linear polyethylene produced by the Ziegler–Natta process, called high-density polyethylene, is a highly crystalline polymer with 4000 to 7000 ethylene units ... greater strength and heat resistance than the branched product of radical-induced polymerization, called low-density polyethylene'), line 29 (HMW, UHMW). 31-7 line 12 (close packing, van der Waals) and line 17 (linear polyethylene highly crystalline). inorgchem 14-4 line 159 (HDPE, LLDPE, UHMWPE uses). 31-8 Table 31.8.1 lines 22/24 (codes 2 and 4) is supplementary. Note: UHMW molecular weight is 3,000,000-6,000,000 amu in orgchem 31-2 but 3.5-7.5 million in inorgchem 14-4. Likely false positive: orgchem 08-10 (radical chain-growth mechanism of polyethylene, no density/branching discussion).

q: What's the oldest inorganic compound people have used? Is it Prussian blue?
expect: The two sections disagree. Section 1.3 says inorganic compounds have been known since antiquity and 'probably the oldest is the deep blue pigment called Prussian blue (Fe4[Fe(CN)6]3)'. Section 9.2 says one of the oldest synthetic pigments is Egyptian blue, CaCuSi4O10, a copper complex used by the Egyptians since the third millennium B.C. (Han blue, the Ba analogue, was found independently in ancient China), and that Prussian blue was only discovered in 1706 by the Berlin painter Diesbach (it gives the formula KFe2(CN)6). A good answer reports both and points out that, on 9.2's dates, Egyptian blue is far older than Prussian blue.

Later, in 1706, the Berlin painter Diesbach would discover another deep blue pigment, Prussian blue: KFe2(CN)6.' The formulas differ too (Fe4[Fe(CN)6]3 vs KFe2(CN)6, the 'soluble' form); 09-6 line 18 (Fe^3+ : [Fe(CN)6]^4- = 4:3) supports 1.3's formula, so the formula is a secondary point, the date is the real conflict. Neither section mentions the other. 'Prussian blue' also appears in 09-6 (coordination framework, no history), a likely partial hit.

q: Using Slater's rules, what effective nuclear charge Z* does a 4s electron in a zinc atom feel? How does that compare with a 3d electron in Zn?
expect: Group the orbitals in order of increasing energy: (1s)(2s,2p)(3s,3p)(3d)(4s,4p). For a 4s electron in Zn ([Ar]3d^10 4s^2): the other 4s electron contributes 0.35; the 18 electrons in shell n - 1 = 3 (3s, 3p, 3d) contribute 0.85 each; the 10 electrons in shells 1 and 2 contribute 1.00 each. S = 0.35 + 18(0.85) + 10(1.00) = 0.35 + 15.3 + 10 = 25.65, so Z* = 30 - 25.65 = 4.35. The book's worked value for a 3d electron in Zn is Z* = 30 - [18(1) + 9(0.35)] = 30 - 21.15 = 8.85, so the 4s electron feels a much smaller effective nuclear charge (about half) than the 3d electrons.
note: 02-2 lines 750-771 (Slater's rules: Z* = Z - S; same group 0.35; for s/p electrons, n - 1 shell 0.85 and lower shells 1.00; d/f electrons shielded 1.00 by everything to the left), Example 2.2.4.1 (F^-, Ne, Na^+, line 783ff) and Exercise 2.2.4.1 (Zn 3d, S = 21.15, Z* = 8.85, lines 805-807). Numbers changed from the book's Zn 3d exercise to the 4s electron. Recomputed: 0.35 + 15.30 + 10.00 = 25.65; 30 - 25.65 = 4.35. Likely false positives: physchem 08-6 (Slater determinants, 21 hits on 'Slater', unrelated), physchem 11-2 (Slater-type orbitals), inorgchem 02-3 and 08-2 (effective nuclear charge trends, no rules).

q: in SF4 why does the lone pair go in an equatorial spot of the trigonal bipyramid instead of an axial one? and what does that do to the shape
expect: SF4 is AX4E: five electron groups (four bonding pairs, one lone pair) arranged as a trigonal bipyramid. Axial positions are more crowded (three neighbours at 90°) than equatorial ones (two at 90°), and lone pairs are more repulsive than bonding pairs. A lone pair placed axially would have three 90° LP-BP repulsions; placed equatorially it has only two, so the equatorial position is more stable. The molecular shape is a seesaw (trigonal bipyramid missing an equatorial vertex), and the lone pair squeezes the F_axial-S-F_axial angle to 173° instead of 180°.
note: 03-2 line 230 (axial groups more crowded; lone pairs prefer equatorial positions because they are more repulsive), line 235 (AX4E1: lone pair equatorial, see saw), lines 243-260 (SF4: 'If we place the lone pair in the axial position, we have three LP-BP repulsions at 90°. If we place it in the equatorial position, we have two'; seesaw; 'The F_axial-S-F_axial angle is 173°'). Distinct from q025 (generic VSEPR with lone pairs, answered by Beginning Chemistry); only inorgchem treats axial vs equatorial. 'SF4' also appears in 03-1 (Lewis structure, expanded octet), 08-11 (sulfur fluorides) and introductory 03-3 (naming), none of which explain the lone-pair placement.

q: Is BeF2 really a linear molecule like its Lewis structure predicts?
expect: Only in the gas phase. At ambient temperature and pressure BeF2 is a quartz-like solid in which Be is four-coordinate and tetrahedral and each F is two-coordinate, bridging Be atoms in an extended 3-D network (Be-F bond length 1.54 Å). The liquid has a fluctuating tetrahedral structure. Above about 1000 °C (at ~1 atm) the vapour contains the linear BeF2 monomer, with a shorter Be-F bond of 1.43 Å, consistent with some Be-F double-bond character. (BeCl2, by contrast, is a 1-D chain polymer in the solid and a Cl-bridged dimer in the gas.)
note: 03-1 section 3.1.4, lines 351-379: Lewis structures predict linear BeX2 (line 357); line 367 'BeF2 is a solid that looks similar to quartz ... The Be is four-coordinate with tetrahedral geometry; each F is two-coordinate and the Be-F bond length is 1.54 Å'; line 371 (liquid; vapour above 1000 °C is a linear monomer with bond length 1.43 Å); lines 377-379 (BeCl2 polymer and dimer). The [Note: corrected] at line 361 (structure on the right, not left) does not affect this answer. 'BeF2' occurs only here and in physchem 10-3 (BeH2 is linear), a likely false positive that discusses the isolated molecule only.

q: What symmetry elements does a tetrahedral molecule like CH4 (point group T_d) have? Does it have any C4 axes?
expect: T_d molecules have the identity, 4 C3 axes (one through each vertex), 3 C2 axes, 3 S4 axes and 6 dihedral mirror planes (σd); there are no C4 axes. As operations, T_d = {E, 8C3, 3C2, 6S4, 6σd}, order 24. CH4 is the textbook example.

q: Can IR spectroscopy tell me whether a square planar ML2(CO)2 complex is the cis or the trans isomer?
expect: Yes. The cis isomer is C_2v; its two C-O stretches reduce to A1 + B1, and both are IR-active and Raman-active, so two CO bands are possible in the IR (and two in the Raman). The trans isomer is D_2h; its C-O stretches reduce to Ag + B_3u. Ag is Raman-active only and B_3u is IR-active only, so the trans isomer gives only one IR band (and one Raman band). Two CO stretching bands therefore rule out a pure sample of the trans isomer.

Raman-active only, while the B_3u ... IR-active only'), summary line 347. Likely false positives: physchem 13-14 and 12-13 (general IR/Raman activity from group theory, no metal carbonyls), analchem 16-1 (IR theory). The mer/fac ML3(CO)3 exercise in the same file has printed band counts flagged by [Note]s (lines 375, 389); this question avoids it.

q: why is B2 paramagnetic? i thought the sigma 2p orbital fills before the pi ones
expect: Because of orbital mixing (s-p mixing). Orbitals of the same symmetry mix even when their energies differ: the two σg orbitals (from 2s and 2p) mix, pushing σg(2s) down and σg(2p) up. Early in period 2 (up to and including N2) this puts σg(2p) above the two degenerate πu(2p) orbitals; from O2 onward σg(2p) lies below πu. So in B2 the last two valence electrons go into the two degenerate bonding πu orbitals, one each with parallel spins: B2 = σg^2 σu*^2 (2s) πu^1 πu^1 (2p). The two unpaired electrons make diboron paramagnetic, which MO theory predicts correctly and Lewis/valence bond pictures do not.
note: inorgchem 05-2 lines 72-79 (mixing of orbitals of like symmetry lowers the lower set and raises the higher), line 105 ('Early in period 2 (up to and including nitrogen), the πu(2p) orbitals are lower in energy than the σg(2p)'), Figure 5.2.3.1 caption line 107, line 113 ('Diboron, B2 [σg^2σu^(*2)(2s)πu^1πu^1(2p)] ... paramagnetic ... a consequence of orbital mixing'). The [Note: corrected] at line 115 changes 'πu^*' to 'πu': the unpaired electrons are in bonding πu orbitals, not antibonding. physchem 09-7 line 124 gives the same ordering argument (σ2pz above π2p for Li2-N2, from 2s-2pz interaction). The question deliberately does not ask for a bond order (q027). Likely false positives: physchem 09-10 (O2 paramagnetism), inorgchem 10-1 (paramagnetism of complexes), orgchem 01-11 (MO basics).

q: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so why does carbon monoxide bind to metal ions through the carbon atom?
expect: Because a ligand acts as a Lewis base using the electrons in its HOMO, and the HOMO of CO is the 3σ orbital, whose electron density is concentrated on the carbon atom. Mixing of the C 2s, C 2pz and O 2pz orbitals raises 3σ and makes it lopsided: it is more heavily distributed toward the less electronegative carbon (larger exterior lobe on C). So carbon, not oxygen, is the better Lewis base and the donor atom, even though the lower-lying 2σ and 1π orbitals are concentrated on oxygen.
note: 05-3 line 84 (mixing of O 2pz with C 2pz and C 2s raises 3σ), line 86 (2σ and 1π weighted toward O), line 98 ('The 3σ orbital is more heavily distributed toward the carbon atom ... caused by the mixing of the carbon 2s orbital'), line 112-114 (reactions at HOMO/LUMO), line 118 ('When CO binds to metal ions, it does so through the carbon atom'), Exercise 5.3.2.2 answer line 128 ('the HOMO is the 3σ orbital ... centered around the carbon atom, thus the carbon atom will be a better Lewis base'). The [Note] at line 120 adds that CO's Lewis structure already puts a lone pair and -1 formal charge on C. Likely false positives: inorgchem 13-4 (CO as a ligand, back-bonding, no HOMO argument), 10-1 (CO vs O2 binding constants to hemoglobin), physchem 09-12 (heteronuclear MO theory).

q: What makes a Lewis acid or base 'hard' or 'soft', and which way does 2TlF + K2S ⇌ Tl2S + 2KF go?
expect: Hard and soft refer to polarizability (Pearson's names for Ahrland, Chatt and Davies' class a and class b). Hard acids and bases are hard to polarize: few valence electrons (polarizing means distorting core electrons) and/or high charge density or electron deficiency; hard acids lie toward the left of the periodic table, with higher oxidation states and/or electron-withdrawing substituents. Soft acids and bases are easily polarized: many valence electrons, low charge density and/or electron-rich; soft acids lie toward the middle/right, with lower oxidation states and/or electron-donating substituents. The HSAB principle says like prefers like, both thermodynamically and kinetically. So 2TlF + K2S ⇌ Tl2S + 2KF lies to the products: soft Tl+ pairs with soft S^2- and hard K+ with hard F-.
note: DISTRACTOR. 'HSAB/hard and soft' (grep 'HSAB\|hard-soft\|hard and soft') hits 06-6 (22), 09-4 (3), 10-1 (2), 06-3 (2), 03-2 (1), 06-4 (1). Only 06-6 defines the classes: line 334 (polarizability; Pearson's hard/soft = class a/b), lines 340-349 (two varieties each of hard and soft), line 354 (periodic-table position, oxidation state, substituents; its [Note: corrected] changes 'electron donating' to 'electron withdrawing' for hard acids), line 408 (HSAB principle), line 419 ('2TlF + K2S ⇌ Tl2S + 2KF' favoring products, itself corrected from 'H2S'). q: What counts as a superacid, what is magic acid made of, and how much stronger is it than sulfuric acid?
expect: A superacid is an acid with greater Brønsted acidity than pure sulfuric acid; since H2SO4 has a Hammett acidity H0 = -12, superacids have H0 < -12. Magic acid is a mixture of SbF5 and FSO3H (fluorosulfonic acid), with H0 of about -24 to -21 (the value depends on the SbF5:FSO3H ratio), i.e. roughly 10^9 to 10^12 times more acidic than sulfuric acid on the Hammett scale; it can even protonate methane to give CH5+. Fluoroantimonic acid (SbF5 + HF) lies in the same range. Superacids dissociate completely because they give extremely stable anions with the charge spread over many electronegative atoms.
note: 06-3 section 6.3.4: line 237 (superacids defined as more acidic than sulfuric acid), line 239 (stable delocalized anions), line 255 ('mixtures of SbF5 and FSO3H called Magic Acid can even protonate methane, which gives a CH5^+ cation'), line 309 (H2SO4 H0 = -12, superacids H0 < -12), Table 6.3.4.1 line 321 ('Magic Acid, F5Sb---FSO3H | -24 to -21'). Line 153 carries [Note: corrected; the source prints "magic acid, a mixture of HF and SbF5" where this reads "magic acid, a mixture of FSO3H and SbF5"]; a correct answer must not call magic acid HF/SbF5 (that is fluoroantimonic acid). Ratio: 10^(-21 - (-12)) to 10^(-24 - (-12)) = 10^9 to 10^12. 'magic acid' and 'Hammett' occur only in 06-3; 06-4 lines 217-219 mention superacid conjugate bases as noncoordinating anions (near miss).

q: why can't you tell whether HCl or HClO4 is the stronger acid if you only test them in water?
expect: Because of the solvent leveling effect. The conjugate acid of the solvent (here H3O+) is the strongest acid that can exist in that solvent: any acid HA significantly stronger than HS+ dissociates essentially completely (HA + S → HS+ + A-). Both HCl and HClO4 are much stronger than H3O+, so in water both ionize completely and look equally strong. To rank them you need a differentiating solvent that is more weakly basic than water, e.g. acetonitrile, in which both only partly dissociate and HClO4 dissociates to a greater extent than HCl. The same leveling limits the strongest base to the solvent's conjugate base.
note: 06-3 section 6.3.10, lines 887-897: line 889 ('The conjugate acid and base of the solvent are the strongest Brønsted acids and bases that can exist in that solvent'), line 895 ('Any acid significantly stronger than HS^+ will act as a strong acid ... This is called the leveling effect ... no way to distinguish the acidity of strong Arrhenius acids like HClO4 and HCl in water ... acetonitrile acts as a differentiating solvent towards HClO4 and HCl'), line 897 (basic leveling). 'leveling' also hits physchem 09-1, 09-4 and 31-6 (energy-level wording, false positives). Beginning Chemistry treats HCl as a strong acid but never discusses leveling.

q: A crystal with planes 0.394 nm apart diffracts X-rays of wavelength 0.147 nm. At what angle does the first-order diffraction appear?
expect: Use the Bragg equation nλ = 2d sin θ with n = 1: sin θ = λ/(2d) = 0.147 nm/(2 × 0.394 nm) = 0.187, so θ = 10.8°. (Leaving out the factor of 2 would give 21.9°, which is wrong.)

q: If you replace a few Ti atoms in TiO2 with niobium, do you get an n-type or a p-type semiconductor? What about Cu2O with some copper missing?
expect: Nb-doped TiO2 is n-type: for substitutions, putting in an atom from further right in the periodic table (Nb has one more valence electron than Ti) adds electrons, so electrons are the majority carriers (F on O sites in TiO2 likewise gives n-type). Copper-deficient Cu1-xO is p-type: cation vacancies give p-type doping (anion vacancies, as in CdS1-x or WO3-x, give n-type), so holes are the majority carriers. Interstitial cations such as Li donate electrons (n-type). By the same logic P in Si is n-type and B in Si is p-type.

Only 07-1 gives the substitution/vacancy rules: line 314 ('adding an atom to the right in the periodic table results in n-type doping, and an atom to the left in p-type doping'), line 316 ('when TiO2 is doped with Nb on some of the Ti sites, or with F on O sites, the result is n-type doping'), line 318 ('Anion vacancies result in n-type doping, and cation vacancies in p-type doping'), line 320 ('copper vacancies in Cu1-xO, which gives a p-type semiconductor'); P and B in Si at lines 293-295. analchem 02-4 line 36 covers only Si/Ge doped with In/Ga (holes) or As/Sb (electrons), so it is a likely false positive that cannot answer the TiO2 or vacancy parts; 07-3 (doped cuprate superconductors) and 09-5 (lanthanide-doped lattices) are others.

q: What kind of bonds hold the bridging hydrogens in diborane, B2H6, and why does it need them?
expect: Three-center two-electron (3c-2e) bonds: each B-H-B bridge holds two electrons shared over three atoms. Diborane is electron-deficient: 2c-2e bonds throughout would need 14 valence electrons but B2H6 has only 12, so the BH3 units dimerize through two B-H-B bridges, giving each boron an octet. The bridge can be described as a molecular orbital built from the three atoms' orbitals (or, in valence bond terms, overlap of H 1s with B sp^3 orbitals).

A correct answer says three-center two-electron, not the printed two-center three-electron. 15-4 line 22: '14 electrons are needed to form 2c,2e-bonds, but only 12 valence electrons are present ... two B-H-B bonds, which have three centers, but only two electrons (3c, 2e bond)'. 03-1 line 399 ('3-center-2-electron bonds') and 08-4 line 139 (E-H-E bonds of group 13 hydrides 'explained as three-center two-electron bonds', Al2H6 scheme) agree. q: why does thallium like to be +1 when aluminum is basically always +3? is the 6s pair really 'inert'?
expect: Down group 13 the lower (n - 2)+ oxidation state becomes more favored: preference for +3 runs Al3+ > Ga3+ > In3+ > Tl3+ and for +1 Al+ < Ga+ < In+ < Tl+, so Al's most stable oxide and chloride are Al2O3 and AlCl3 but Tl's are Tl2O and TlCl. This is called the inert pair effect, as if the ns^2 electrons did not take part in bonding. The book calls the name a misnomer: the ns electrons do not get significantly lower in energy down the group, and the cost of removing the 'inert pair' (IE2 + IE3) is highest for B, drops ~25% to Al and then stays roughly constant (Al 4,560; Tl 4,849 kJ/mol). What changes is that M-X bonds get weaker as bonds lengthen (M-Cl: Al 494, Ga 481, In 439, Tl 372.8 kJ/mol), so for heavy Tl the bond energy gained no longer pays for oxidizing away the ns^2 pair, and the lower oxidation state wins.
note: 08-6 section 8.6.2: line 579 (preference for an oxidation state two lower; 'inert pair effect'), lines 589-599 (Al^3+ > Ga^3+ > In^3+ > Tl^3+; Al2O3/AlCl3 vs Tl2O/TlCl), line 601 (classical explanation), lines 603-611 ('the term inert pair effect is a misnomer'; due to decreasing bond energies), Table 8.6.2.2 line 623 (IE2 + IE3: B 6,086; Al 4,560; Ga 4,942; In 4,524; Tl 4,849 kJ/mol), Table 8.6.2.3 (M-Cl 536, 494, 481, 439, 372.8), line 631 (conclusion). 'inert pair' occurs only in 08-6. 'inert' alone hits 12-2 (26, kinetically inert complexes), 08-14 (inert noble gases) and physchem rotor files (moment of inertia), all false positives.

q: What did Werner mean by a metal's primary and secondary valence, and what evidence from the PtCl4·nNH3 compounds supported it?
expect: Werner proposed two kinds of valence: the primary valence is the oxidation state (the positive charge on the metal ion) and the secondary valence is the coordination number (the total number of ligands bound to the metal). His conductivity and AgCl-precipitation data on PtCl4·nNH3 (n = 2-6) fit Pt with primary valence 4 and secondary valence 6: PtCl4·6NH3 conducted most (523 ohm^-1, 5 ions, 4 Cl- precipitated by Ag+) and is [Pt(NH3)6]Cl4; each NH3 lost moves one Cl- into the coordination sphere, down to PtCl4·2NH3, a neutral non-conducting [Pt(NH3)2Cl4] (0 ions, no free Cl-). The rival Blomstrand-Jørgensen chain theory equated valence with coordination number.
note: DISTRACTOR. 'Werner' hits 09-2 (14), 01-3 (2), 09-4 (2), 10-2 (1) and physchem 01-9, 14-2, 14-3, 25-8, 26-13 (1 each: Werner Heisenberg and other people named Werner). Only 09-2 explains primary/secondary valence: line 16 (valence and coordination number had been thought identical; chain theory), Table 9.2.1 lines 28-34 (PtCl4·6NH3 523, 5, 4 ... PtCl4·2NH3 0, 0, 0), line 36 ('primary valence (oxidation state) ... secondary valence (coordination number)'), equations lines 38-46. q: In coordination and organometallic names, what is the difference between the κ, η and μ symbols, e.g. thiocyanato-κN, η^5-C5H5 and μ3-CO?
expect: κ (kappa) names the donor atom(s) of a ligand: thiocyanato-κN means NCS- bound through N (M-NCS), thiocyanato-κS bound through S (M-SCN); κ^n gives the number of attached atoms when they are not directly bonded to each other (usually σ-type coordination of a multidentate ligand). η^n (eta, hapticity) gives the number of contiguous, bonded atoms of a π system bound to the metal: η^5-C5H5 is pentahapto cyclopentadienyl (all five carbons), and Cp or allyl can also bind η^1 or η^3. μ (mu) marks a bridging ligand: μ_n bridges n metals, with the subscript usually omitted for n = 2, so μ3-CO is a carbonyl bridging three metals and μ2-CO (μ-CO) one bridging two; a terminal CO needs no μ.
note: Exact-token: κ vs η vs μ. 09-3 lines 336-345 ('thiocyanato-S or thiocyanato-κS', 'thiocyanato-N or thiocyanato-κN'; the κ 'k-term'), Table 9.3.4 line 351-355 (κ^n: attached atoms not directly connected, σ-type; η^n: coordinated atoms all connected, π-type, monohapto/dihapto/trihapto; μ_n bridging, n omitted when 2). 13-2 lines 12-16 (η, Cp η^1/η^3/η^5), line 20 (allyl η^1/η^3), line 30 ('For a ligand that bridges n metal ions, the symbol is written as μn ... omitted when n = 2'; terminal, μ2, μ3 carbonyls). 09-4 line 78 has [Note: corrected; the source prints "binds through its nitrogen (μ-N)" where this reads "binds through its nitrogen (κN)"]: confusing κ with μ is the trap. Note 09-3's table says n in μ_n is 'the number of atoms bridged' while 13-2 says metal ions bridged; the latter is meant. 'κ' also hits physchem 25-6 (Debye-Hückel κ), 22-3 and 28-8 (other quantities), all false positives.

q: Using the textbook's values of Δ_o and pairing energy, is [Fe(OH2)6]^3+ high spin or low spin? What would its LFSE be in each case?
expect: Fe^3+ is d^5. Table 1 gives Δ_o = 14,000 cm^-1 for Fe(OH2)6^3+ and Table 4 gives a total pairing energy Π = 30,000 cm^-1. Pairing costs more than promoting an electron to e_g (30,000 > 14,000), so the complex is high spin, t2g^3 eg^2, with 5 unpaired electrons (spin-only moment 5.92 BM). LFSE (high spin) = [0.6(2) - 0.4(3)]Δ_o = 0Δ_o = 0. LFSE (low spin, t2g^5) = [0.6(0) - 0.4(5)]Δ_o = -2.0Δ_o = -28,000 cm^-1, but reaching it would mean pairing two extra electrons (ΔE(ls - hs) = -2Δ_o + 2Πc), which the large pairing energy does not repay.

Fe(III) is not one of the book's worked cases; recomputed: 0.6×2 - 0.4×3 = 0; -0.4×5 = -2.0; -2.0 × 14,000 = -28,000 cm^-1. Not the q115 topic (Fe(II), [Fe(CN)6]^4- vs [Fe(H2O)6]^2+).

q: What spin-only magnetic moment would you expect for a Cu^2+ complex, and what value does the spin-plus-orbital formula give?
expect: Cu^2+ is d^9, with one unpaired electron (n = 1, S = 1/2). Spin-only: μ_so = √(n(n + 2)) = √3 = 1.73 BM. With orbital angular momentum: fill the d orbitals to maximize L (ml = 2, 2, 1, 1, 0, 0, -1, -1, -2), so L = 2, and μ_(S+L) = g√(S(S + 1) + (1/4)L(L + 1)) = 2√(3/4 + 6/4) = 2√(9/4) = 3.00 BM. Observed moments usually fall between μ_so and μ_(S+L).
note: 10-1 section 10.1.2: μ_so = g√(S(S + 1)) (line 235), table of μ_so (n = 1 → 1.73 BM, line 244), μ_so = √(n(n + 2)) (line 256), μ_(s+L) = g√(S(S + 1) + (1/4)L(L + 1)) (line 262) with the Co^2+ worked example (L = 3, 5.20 vs 3.87 BM; observed values in between, line 270); Exercises 10.1.2.2-3 (line 318ff) do V^4+, Cr^2+, Ni^2+, Co^3+, Mn^2+, Fe^2+, Cr^3+, V^3+ but not Cu^2+. Recomputed: √3 = 1.732; L = 4 + 2 + 0 - 2 - 2 = 2; 2√(0.75 + 1.5) = 3.000. (11-2 line 351 independently gives Cu^2+ as d^9, ^2D, i.e. L = 2.) Corpus inconsistency, not used here: Exercise 10.1.2.2 treats Co^3+ as low-spin (n = 0) while 10.1.2.3 uses S = 2 (high-spin). 'spin-only' occurs only in 10-1.

q: How much does the entropy increase when three ethylenediamine ligands replace the six ammonias in [Ni(NH3)6]^2+?
expect: The book gives two different values for the same reaction, [Ni(NH3)6]^2+ + 3en ⇌ [Ni(en)3]^2+ + 6NH3. Section 10.1.1 gives ΔS° = 184.9 J mol^-1 K^-1, i.e. -TΔS° = -55.1 kJ mol^-1 at 298 K, with ΔH° = -12.1 kJ mol^-1 (so entropy, not enthalpy, drives K = 4.7 × 10^9). Section 12.2 says the entropy increases by 88 J K^-1 mol^-1. Both attribute it to the chelate effect: the number of molecules goes from 4 to 7. A good answer reports both values and their sections rather than picking one silently.
note: Within-book contradiction (inorgchem). 10-1 line 96 'ΔS° = 184.9 J mol^-1 K^-1', line 98 '-TΔS° = -55.1 kJ mol^-1', line 94 'ΔH° = -12.1', lines 108-114 (4 vs 7 molecules; 'chelate effect'). 12-2 line 271 ('increases the number of molecules from four to seven, and hence the entropy increases, in this case by 88 J K^-1 and mol^-1'); the corpus [Note] at line 273 already flags that 10.1.1 gives 184.9 and the source does not reconcile them. Recomputed: 298 × 184.9 = 55.1 kJ; 298 × 88 = 26.2 kJ, so the two values imply TΔS differing by about a factor of two. 12-4 (kinetic chelate effect, lines 201-225) is a near miss with no ΔS value. Distinct from q006 (coordination number of [Co(en)3]^3+).

q: How big is Δ_t compared with Δ_o, and why are tetrahedral complexes often more intensely coloured than octahedral ones?
expect: Δ_t = (4/9)Δ_o, so for comparable ligands the tetrahedral splitting is less than half the octahedral one (e.g. Δ_o = 18,000 cm^-1 would correspond to Δ_t = 8,000 cm^-1); tetrahedral complexes therefore absorb at lower energy and longer wavelength. They are often more intensely coloured because their d-d transitions are Laporte-allowed: the Laporte rule (g ↔ u only) applies only to centrosymmetric complexes, and a tetrahedron has no inversion centre (its terms carry no g subscripts), whereas octahedral d-d transitions are Laporte-forbidden. Mixing of s and p orbitals with the d orbitals in a tetrahedral complex also relaxes the restriction. (The splitting pattern is inverted, so a d^n tetrahedral ion is read from the d^(10-n) Tanabe-Sugano diagram.)
note: Exact-token: Δ_t vs Δ_o (and 'Laporte'). 11-3 line 374 (tetrahedral d-d transitions Laporte-allowed, octahedral forbidden; no g subscripts), line 376 (s/p mixing), line 378 ('It is also worth noting that Δt = (4/9)Δo. The smaller Δ ... absorb at a lower energy and longer wavelength'), line 384 (d^n tetrahedral uses d^(10-n) diagram; its [Note: corrected] replaces [Ni(H2O)6]^2+ with [NiCl4]^2-), Laporte rule lines 46 and 54-56. Numerical example recomputed: 4/9 × 18,000 = 8,000. 'Δt' with 4/9 also appears only in a [Note] in 10-4 line 458 (AOM Δ_t = (4/3)eσ - (16/9)eπ); 10-3 lines 596-605 argue qualitatively that the tetrahedral splitting is smaller. Likely false positives: analchem 14-2 (Δ_oct for Cu(H2O)6^2+, no Δ_t), physchem 09-15 (one 'Laporte' hit, molecular term symbols).

q: What are the ground-state free-ion term symbols, including J, for Mn^2+ and for Ni^2+?
expect: Mn^2+ is d^5: one electron in each of ml = 2, 1, 0, -1, -2, all spins parallel, so S = 5/2 (multiplicity 2S + 1 = 6) and L = 2 + 1 + 0 - 1 - 2 = 0 (an S term): ^6S. The shell is exactly half-filled, so there is only one J = L + S = 5/2: ^6S_5/2. Ni^2+ is d^8: ml = 2, 1, 0 doubly occupied and -1, -2 singly, so S = 1 (multiplicity 3) and L = 2(2) + 2(1) + 2(0) - 1 - 2 = 3 (F): ^3F. The shell is more than half-filled, so the lowest state has the largest J = L + S = 4: ^3F_4.
note: 11-2 lines 287-292 (Hund's first two rules), lines 300-323 (shortcut: fill highest ml first, unpaired before paired; worked for Cr^3+ d^3 → ^4F), Exercise 11.2.1.3 (Ti^2+ ^3F, Ti^3+ ^2D, Cu^2+ ^2D, lines 345-353), lines 361-373 (J = L + S ... |L - S|; Hund's third rule: less than half-filled lowest J, half-filled only one J, more than half-filled largest J). physchem 08-10 states the same three rules (line 21) and works Ti^2+ d^2 → ^3F2 (line 77). The book does neither d^5 nor d^8; recomputed with a script: d^5 S = 2.5, L = 0, J = 2.5; d^8 S = 1, L = 3, J = 4. 10-1 Exercise 10.1.2.3 also gets L = 3, S = 1 for Ni^2+ (line 330). Likely false positives: 11-3 (d^2 terms ^3F, ^3P for Tanabe-Sugano), physchem 08-8/08-9 (general term symbols), 09-14/09-15 (molecular term symbols).

q: how come you get cisplatin when you add ammonia to PtCl4^2-, but transplatin when you add chloride to Pt(NH3)4^2+?
expect: Because of the trans effect: in square planar complexes the ligand trans to a strong trans-director is replaced fastest, so the products are under kinetic, not thermodynamic, control. Cl- has a stronger trans effect than NH3. Starting from [PtCl4]^2-, the first NH3 replaces a Cl-; the second substitution then takes a Cl- that is trans to another Cl- (not the one trans to NH3), giving cis-[PtCl2(NH3)2], cisplatin. Starting from [Pt(NH3)4]^2+, after the first Cl- enters, the NH3 trans to that Cl- is replaced next, giving trans-[PtCl2(NH3)2], transplatin. In both routes the ligand replaced is trans to a chloride. Strong σ-donors (e.g. H-, CH3-, PR3) weaken the bond trans to them by competing for the same metal p orbital; strong π-acceptors (e.g. CO) stabilize the trigonal-bipyramidal five-coordinate intermediate with themselves and the leaving trans ligand in the equatorial plane.
note: 12-7 lines 9-30 (cisplatin vs transplatin syntheses: tetraammine + chloride gives trans-platin; tetrachloroplatinate + ammonia gives cis-platin), Exercise 12.7.1 (associative, square planar, kinetic control, lines 34-42), line 44 ('the ligand that gets replaced is trans to a chloride. It is not trans to an ammonia'), line 48 (definition), rate table lines 52-61 (k_obs PMe3 0.20 s^-1 down to Cl- 3.5 × 10^-6 s^-1), lines 101-104 (σ-donor explanation), lines 123-131 (π-acceptor explanation). 'trans effect' occurs only in 12-7 (10) and 14-1 (1). Likely false positives: 13-3 (cisplatin electron count, 16 e), 09-4 (cis/trans isomers of square planar complexes), 12-6 (square planar substitution kinetics without the trans series).

q: What does it mean for a metal complex to be labile or inert? Is an inert complex the same thing as a stable one?
expect: Labile and inert are kinetic terms about how fast ligands are substituted. Taube suggested: kinetically labile complexes react with a half-life of one minute or less (t_1/2 < 1 min); kinetically inert (non-labile) ones have t_1/2 > 1 min. Stable/unstable are thermodynamic terms, and the two are independent: [Fe(H2O)5Cl]^2+ has a large formation constant (thermodynamically stable) but is labile, while [Co(NH3)6]^3+ is unstable in acidic water (it should decompose to [Co(H2O)6]^3+) yet decomposes slowly because it is inert. Examples in the book: [Ni(OH2)6]^2+ and [Cu(OH2)6]^2+ substitution with NH3 are labile, [Cr(OH2)6]^3+ is inert. Lability depends on LFSE (empty e_g, e.g. d^3 and low-spin d^6, means inert), charge density and the kinetic chelate effect.
note: DISTRACTOR. 'labile' hits 12-2 (most), inorgchem 09-6 (1: 'labile (substitutable) ligands' in framework synthesis) and analchem 25-7 (~10: 'labile metals' in voltammetric speciation, a different sense). Only 12-2 defines the terms: table lines 83-87, line 93 (Taube, t_1/2 < 1 min), line 94 (inert, t_1/2 > 1 min), line 96 (kinetic vs thermodynamic; [Fe(H2O)5Cl]^2+ stable but labile, [Co(NH3)6]^3+ unstable but inert), lines 129-135 (LFSE, Coulombic attraction, denticity), Exercise 12.2.2.3 table (line 179ff). The corpus [Note] at line 89 flags that the table's parenthetical times do not follow from its rate constants; a good answer should not quote those times. 'inert' alone also hits 08-6 (inert pair), 08-14 (inert gases), physchem rotor pages (inertia).

q: Count the valence electrons in CpMn(CO)3 (Cp = η^5-C5H5) and in nickelocene, NiCp2. Which one obeys the 18-electron rule, and what would you expect the other to do?
expect: Donor pair (oxidation state) method, with Cp- as a six-electron L2X donor and CO as a two-electron L donor. CpMn(CO)3 is neutral: one Cp- makes Mn +1; Mn is in group 7, so Mn(I) is d^6; total = 6 + 6 (Cp) + 3 × 2 (CO) = 18 electrons: coordinatively saturated. NiCp2: two Cp- make Ni +2; Ni is in group 10, so Ni(II) is d^8; total = 8 + 6 + 6 = 20 electrons (neutral-atom method: 10 + 5 + 5 = 20). Nickelocene is coordinatively oversaturated (> 18), so it should tend to lose ligands and/or be oxidized, much as 19-electron cobaltocene readily gives up an electron.
note: 13-3: donor pair method lines 20-25 (oxidation state, d count = group number - oxidation state, two electrons per ligand bond) and neutral atom method lines 47-54; 18-electron rule line 78; definitions line 84-88 ('Coordinatively oversaturated: ... >18 electrons. These complexes tend to lose ligands and become oxidized'); Cp as 'a polydentate, six-electron L2X ligand' and CO as two-electron L (line 152); total electron count = d electrons + ligand electrons (line 156, CpFe(CO)2Et = 6 + (6 + 2 + 2 + 2) = 18); cobaltocene 7 + (6 + 6) = 19, a one-electron reducing agent (line 176). Numbers changed from the book's Fe/Mo/Co examples. Recomputed: (7 - 1) + 6 + 6 = 18; (10 - 2) + 6 + 6 = 20; 10 + 5 + 5 = 20. 'nickelocene' and 'CpMn(CO)3' do not appear in the corpus. Likely false positives: 13-1 (ferrocene history), 13-5 (Cp bonding by group theory), 15-2 (fragment electron counts for the isolobal analogy).

q: What's the difference between a Fischer carbene and a Schrock carbene?
expect: Both have a metal-carbon double bond, but they are deconstructed differently. A Fischer carbene has π-acidic ligands (e.g. CO) on the metal and π-basic substituents (e.g. OR, NR2) on the carbene carbon; it is treated as an L-type (neutral two-electron) ligand, so it does not change the metal's oxidation state, and its carbene carbon is electrophilic because back-bonding is weak (zwitterionic resonance forms; chemistry resembles esters/amides). A Schrock carbene has 'neutral' substituents (R = H, alkyl) on a metal that is a good back-bonder (no π-acidic ligands, not an electronegative late metal); it is treated as an X2-type (dianionic) ligand, which raises the metal's oxidation state by two, and its carbene carbon is nucleophilic because back-bonding piles electron density onto it. Many real carbenes are in between.
note: 13-6 line 163 (Fischer, Schrock carbenes and vinylidenes all have M=C), line 171 (two ways to deconstruct the M=C bond: L-type carbenoid or X2), line 177 ('When the metal possesses π-acidic ligands and the R groups are π-basic, the complex is best described as an L-type Fischer carbene ... When the ligands are "neutral" (R = H, alkyl) and the metal is a good backbonder ... X2-type Schrock carbene'), line 179 (Schrock carbon nucleophilic, Fischer carbon electrophilic), line 195 (many intermediate), line 257 (Fischer carbenes like carboxylic acid derivatives). 13-2 table lists 'Carbene (alkylidene) | X2'. 'Fischer' also hits orgchem chapter 25 (Fischer projections, 24 hits in 25-2) and orgchem carbene pages (08-9: free carbenes, cyclopropanation), likely false positives; 14-3 (Schrock and Grubbs metathesis catalysts) is a near miss.

q: What is Wilkinson's catalyst, what reaction does it catalyze, and what is the actual active catalyst?
expect: Wilkinson's catalyst is the square planar rhodium(I) complex chlorotris(triphenylphosphine)rhodium(I), RhCl(PPh3)3, an effective catalyst for hydrogenating olefins. It is a precatalyst: it reversibly loses one PPh3 to give the actual catalyst, chlorobis(triphenylphosphine)rhodium(I), RhCl(PPh3)2 (which is also in equilibrium with its dimer). The cycle combines oxidative addition of H2 (to a Rh(III) dihydride), olefin binding and migratory insertion into Rh-H, and reductive elimination of the alkane, regenerating RhCl(PPh3)2; branched alkyls can undergo β-hydride elimination as a side reaction.
note: 14-3 section 14.3.5, line 270: 'Wilkinson's catalyst is the square planar chloro tris(triphenylphosphine) rhodium(I) complex. This molecule is actually a precatalyst that becomes the actual catalyst when it statistically loses a triphenylphosphine ligand producing chloro bis(triphenylphosphine) rhodium(I)'; the rest of the paragraph covers H2 oxidative addition, olefin insertion, β-hydride elimination of the branched alkyl and reductive elimination of the linear alkane. 'Wilkinson' also appears in 09-5 line 153 (lists [RhCl(PPh3)3] as a square planar example, no catalysis), 13-1 line 127 (Geoffrey Wilkinson and ferrocene), 10-1, 02-3 and 08-13 (Cotton and Wilkinson references): all likely false positives.

q: Use Wade's rules to predict the structure type of the borane B6H10.
expect: Valence electrons: 6 B × 3 + 10 H × 1 = 28. Subtract 2 for each of the six B-H vertex units: 28 - 12 = 16 skeletal electrons = 8 skeletal electron pairs (SEP). Parent deltahedron: n = SEP - 1 = 7 vertices (a pentagonal bipyramid). B6H10 has 6 boron atoms = n - 1, so it is a nido cluster: a pentagonal bipyramid with one vertex missing. This matches the formula pattern BnH(n+4) (B6H10 = B6H6+4) with n + 2 = 8 SEP for nido boranes.
note: 15-4 Wade's rules lines 34-55 (3 e per B, 1 per H; subtract 2 per vertex unit; SEP = remaining/2; n = SEP - 1; closo n, nido n - 1, arachno n - 2, hypho n - 3 vertex atoms, the latter fixed by a [Note: corrected] that had printed 'n boron atoms' for every class), table line 59 ('Bn Hn + 4 | n+2 | nido'), nido description line 79, worked examples B5H11 (arachno, n = 7 pentagonal bipyramid, line 106), B5H9 (nido, n = 6) and B6H6^2- (closo). Recomputed: 18 + 10 = 28; 28 - 12 = 16; 16/2 = 8; n = 7; 6 = n - 1 → nido. B6H10 does not appear in the corpus. Likely false positive: 08-6 (borane clusters, closo/nido/arachno described qualitatively; its decaborane passage still calls B10H14 'arachno' after a correction to 'nido', see report).

q: Roughly how uncertain is the speed of an electron confined to a hydrogen atom about 1 × 10^-10 m across? Use the minimum-uncertainty form of the Heisenberg principle.
expect: Take the uncertainty in position as half the diameter, Δx = ±5 × 10^-11 m (the book uses half the range, as for a particle in a box of length L, where Δx = L/2). From Δp_x Δx ≥ ħ/2 with Δp = mΔv (the mass is not uncertain): Δv ≥ ħ/(2mΔx) = (1.0545718 × 10^-34 kg m^2/s)/[(2)(9.109383 × 10^-31 kg)(5 × 10^-11 m)] = 1.16 × 10^6 m/s. This is larger than for an electron confined to a magnesium atom of 150 pm radius (Example 1.9.1: 3.9 × 10^5 m/s), as expected because the hydrogen atom is smaller. The principle sets only a minimum uncertainty; there is no upper limit.
note: Physical Chemistry 1.9, Exercise 1.9.2 (line 142) with its worked answer at lines 148-154; ΔpxΔx ≥ ħ/2 at line 61, the Δx = L/2 convention at line 74, the Mg example at line 101, the comparison at line 156. Misprints: [Note: corrected; the source prints "as ±5 × 10^−10 m" where this reads "as ±5 × 10^−11 m"] (line 150) and [Note: corrected; the source prints "Δv = 1.15 × 10^6 km/s" where this reads "Δv = 1.16 × 10^6 m/s"] (line 154); in km/s the electron would be faster than light, and the printed 5 × 10^-10 m would give 1.16 × 10^5 m/s. A correct answer gives the corrected 1.16 × 10^6 m/s and does not repeat the printed km/s value. Arithmetic: 1.0545718e-34/(2 × 9.109383e-31 × 5e-11) = 1.158e6 m/s. Likely false positives: physchem 14-2 and 14-3 (a misplaced uncertainty-principle passage, ΔpΔx ≥ ħ/2 and a baseball-vs-electron exercise with no answer, under NMR titles), 03-8 (uncertainties computed from particle-in-a-box wavefunctions), 04-6 (general commutator form), inorgchem 02-2 (mentions Heisenberg only).

q: An iron bar heated in a fire first glows deep red at about 900 K. Using Wien's displacement law, at what wavelength is its thermal emission most intense, and is that peak actually in the red?
expect: λ_max = b/T with Wien's displacement constant b = 2.898 × 10^-3 m K: λ_max = (2.898 × 10^-3 m K)/(900 K) = 3.22 × 10^-6 m = 3.22 μm. That is in the infrared, not the visible (red light is about 6.6 × 10^-7 m): thermal radiation spans a wide range of wavelengths and λ_max is only its peak, so the deep-red glow is the short-wavelength tail of the spectrum. Because λ_max is inversely proportional to T, the colour shifts to orange, yellow and finally blue as the temperature rises (10,000 K or more puts the peak in the ultraviolet). For comparison the book's examples give 5.1 × 10^-7 m for the Sun at 5700 K and 9.5 μm for a body at 305 K.
note: Physical Chemistry 1.1: λ_max = b/T (line 117) with b = 2.898 × 10^-3 m K (line 119; the [Note: corrected] at line 121 records the misprint 2.89); 'when an iron is heated in a fire ... the first visible radiation (at around 900 K) is deep red' (line 113); colours of 4.0/5.6/6.6 × 10^-7 m (line 169); thermal radiation spans a wide range and λ_max is only the peak (line 171); Examples 1.1.2 (305 K -> 9.5 μm, line 147) and 1.1.3 (5700 K -> 5.1 × 10^-7 m, line 167). Temperature changed from the book's examples. Arithmetic: 2.898e-3/900 = 3.220e-6 m. Caution for grading: the frequency form, ν_max = (5.879 × 10^10 Hz/K)(900 K) = 5.29 × 10^13 Hz (line 111), is a different peak (c/ν_max = 5.67 μm), so it should not be presented as the wavelength of maximum emission. 'Wien' occurs only in physchem 1.1 across the five books. Near-misses: physchem 1.2 (Planck's law), introductory 8.3 (a hot object gives a continuous spectrum, no Wien law).

q: why can a guitar string that's clamped at both ends only vibrate at certain frequencies? and what's a normal mode or an overtone?
expect: Solving the classical wave equation by separation of variables, u(x,t) = X(x)T(t). Clamping both ends imposes the boundary conditions X(0) = X(L) = 0. Only oscillatory solutions (separation constant K = −p^2 < 0) can satisfy them: X(x) = C cos(px) + D sin(px); X(0) = 0 forces C = 0 and X(L) = 0 forces sin(pL) = 0, so pL = nπ, i.e. p = nπ/L with n = 1, 2, 3, ... (n = 0 is the trivial solution). The allowed shapes are standing waves X_n(x) = D sin(nπx/L), and the time part then oscillates at ω_n = nvπ/L, i.e. ν_n = nv/(2L), so only these discrete frequencies occur; n behaves like a quantum number. Each u_n(x,t) = [G_n cos(ω_n t) + H_n sin(ω_n t)] sin(nπx/L) is a normal mode; n = 1 is the fundamental and the higher modes are overtones (harmonics). Because the wave equation is linear, the general motion of the string is a superposition (sum) of normal modes. Modes with more spatial curvature (higher n) oscillate faster.
note: Physical Chemistry 2.4: K = −p^2 (line 25), pL = nπ (line 119), X(x) = D sin(nπx/L) and the 'quantum number' remark (lines 127-129), ω_n = nvπ/L (line 146), Principle of Superposition (line 189), 'Each un(x, t) solution is called a normal mode ... The first term with n = 1 is typically called the fundamental and each subsequent modes is called an overtone or harmonic' (line 197), ν_n = nv/(2L) (line 201). Section 2.3 lines 50-79 repeats the boundary-condition argument (pL = nπ) without the frequencies or the normal-mode terms. Casual phrasing. Near-misses: 2.2 (sets up separation of variables), 2.5 (membranes, two quantum numbers), physchem 3.5 line 126 (particle-in-a-box states compared with the modes of a violin string).

q: An electron is trapped in a cubic box 0.500 nm on a side. What are the energies of its ground level and its first excited level, how many states share each energy, and what photon wavelength would take it from one to the other?
note: Physical Chemistry 3.9: E(nx,ny,nz) (line 127), E(1,1,1) = 3h^2/8mL^2 non-degenerate (lines 137-139), the first excited state (2,1,1)/(1,2,1)/(1,1,2) = 6h^2/8mL^2, 'three-fold or triply degenerate' (lines 141-145), Table 3.9.1 (lines 157-158). q: What does the commutator of position and momentum, [x̂, p̂], equal, and what uncertainty relation follows from it?
expect: [x̂, p̂] = x̂p̂ − p̂x̂ = iħ (−iħ is the reverse order, [p̂, x̂]). For two operators that do not commute, the general uncertainty principle is σ_A σ_B ≥ (1/2)|∫ψ*[ÂB̂ − B̂Â]ψ dτ|. With [x̂, p̂] = iħ the right-hand side is (1/2)|iħ| = ħ/2, so σ_x σ_px ≥ ħ/2. Because x̂ and p̂ do not commute, position and momentum cannot both be measured to arbitrary precision; operators that do commute can share eigenfunctions, and their quantities can be measured simultaneously with no limit on the uncertainty.

Without the factor 1/2 the bound would come out as ħ instead of ħ/2. A correct answer gives [x̂, p̂] = iħ and the ħ/2 bound, matching ΔpxΔx ≥ ħ/2 in 1.9 (line 61). q: NaH absorbs at 2.94 × 10^11 Hz for its J = 0 → 1 rotational transition. In the rigid-rotor model, where do the J = 1 → 2 and J = 2 → 3 lines fall, what is the spacing between neighbouring lines, and what is the rotational constant B in cm^-1?

q: If you cool a molecule toward absolute zero, do its atoms stop vibrating? What is the zero-point energy of a vibrating bond?
expect: No. A quantum harmonic oscillator has equally spaced levels E_v = (v + 1/2)ħω = (v + 1/2)hν, v = 0, 1, 2, ..., so the lowest allowed energy is E_0 = ħω/2 (hν/2), not zero: the atoms must be moving even in the lowest vibrational state. This residual ground-state energy is the zero-point energy (zero-point motion), 'the lowest possible energy that a quantum mechanical physical system may have', in direct contrast with a classical oscillator, whose lowest energy is zero. Example from the book: for H35Cl, with its fundamental at 2886 cm^-1, ω = 5.44 × 10^14 rad/s and E_0 = (1/2)ħω = 2.87 × 10^-20 J.

This phenomenon is called the zero-point energy or the zero-point motion' (line 31); definition box (line 63). The worked HCl value is 5.5 lines 145-155 (the [Note: corrected] at line 155 records the printed 2.916 × 10^-20 J; a correct answer uses 2.87 × 10^-20 J).
