q: is the electron in a hydrogen atom actually orbiting the nucleus like in the Bohr model? how is the Schrödinger hydrogen atom different from Bohr's?
expect: No well-defined orbit exists in the Schrödinger picture. The book lists three differences: (1) the Schrödinger model gives no orbits; the wavefunctions only give the probability of finding the electron at various directions and distances from the proton (|ψ|^2 is a probability density). (2) Angular momentum is quantized differently: Bohr postulated m_e v r = nħ, integer units of ħ, whereas the Schrödinger model gives a magnitude of √(l(l + 1))ħ, which is zero for l = 0 (s) states - an electron with zero angular momentum cannot be circling the proton. (3) The quantum numbers n, l and m_l arise naturally from the boundary conditions in solving the equation, while Bohr had to postulate quantized states. Both models give the same energy levels, E_n = −μe^4/(8ε0^2 h^2 n^2), but the Schrödinger model agrees with experiment over a much wider range of applications. (The uncertainty principle likewise rules out a fixed circular path.)
note: Physical Chemistry 6.4 'Bohr Theory vs. Schrödinger Theory' (lines 129-135), energy formula (line 127), Exercise 6.4.3 on zero angular momentum (line 139); Bohr's postulate m_e v r = nħ in 1.8 (line 118); |L| = √(l(l + 1))ħ also in 6.3 (line 76); 1.9 line 158 (uncertainty principle showed Bohr's fixed circular path was obsolete). Casual phrasing. Near-misses: inorgchem 2.1 and 2.2 (history of the Bohr model and its failure, without this three-point comparison), introductory 8.3 (Bohr-style energy levels), physchem 6.2 Exercise answer giving √(l(l+1))ħ for 3d.

q: my variational calculation for helium gave an energy lower than the experimental one. is that even possible? what does the variational principle actually guarantee?
expect: It should not happen. The variational theorem says that for a time-independent Hamiltonian, the energy computed with any trial wavefunction and the exact Hamiltonian, E_trial = ⟨ψ_trial|Ĥ|ψ_trial⟩/⟨ψ_trial|ψ_trial⟩, is greater than or equal to the true ground-state energy: E_trial ≥ E_true, so it is an upper bound, equal only when the trial function is the true wavefunction. An answer below the experimental helium energy, E_true = −(I1 + I2) = −(24.59 + 54.42) eV = −79.01 eV (−2.90372 Eh), signals an error rather than a better wavefunction. The method: choose a trial function with adjustable parameters, evaluate E_trial, and minimize it. For helium with effective nuclear charge ζ, E_trial(ζ) = Eh(ζ^2 − 27ζ/8), minimized at ζ = 27/16 = 1.6875, giving −77.48 eV, about 2% above experiment; better trial functions approach from above (−2.84766, −2.86035, −2.87566, −2.89112 (Hylleraas r12 term), −2.90143 Eh vs −2.90372 Eh).
note: Physical Chemistry 7.1: helium I1 = 24.59 eV, I2 = 54.42 eV, E_true = −79.01 eV (lines 27-41, [Note: corrected] at 43); 'the expectation value ... using an approximate wavefunction and the exact Hamiltonian operator will be higher than or equal to the true energy' (line 110); E_trial ≥ E_true (line 112); 'an upper bound to the true ground state energy' (line 120); equality only for the true wavefunction (line 127); ζ = 27/16 and −77.483 eV (lines 165-175). 8.2 lines 96-192: five trial wavefunctions, all above −2.90372 Eh. Casual phrasing; the student's premise is wrong. Near-misses: 7.2 (linear variational method, secular determinant), 7.4 (perturbation theory, which is not bounded), 11.2 line 34 (basis-set energy 'larger than the exact energy'), 6.7 (helium cannot be solved exactly).

q: Is the ground state of the oxygen atom ^3P_2 or ^3P_0? And what about carbon, which also has a ^3P ground term?
expect: Oxygen (2p^4) is ^3P_2; carbon (2p^2) is ^3P_0. Both have a ^3P ground term by Hund's first two rules (largest S, so a triplet; then largest L, so P). L = 1 and S = 1 give J = 2, 1, 0. Hund's third rule picks the level: for a subshell less than half filled (carbon) the smallest J is lowest, ^3P_0; for a subshell more than half filled (oxygen) the largest J is lowest, ^3P_2. (Nitrogen, exactly half filled, is ^4S_3/2.)
note: Physical Chemistry 8.10: Hund's rules (lines 19-21), Exercise 8.10.3 answers 'C ... O ... ^3 P0, ^4 S_3/2, ^3 P2' (lines 83-92). Inorganic Chemistry 11.2 lines 365-375: carbon's ^3P splits into ^3P0, ^3P1, ^3P2 and Hund's third rule makes ^3P0 lowest for a less-than-half-filled p subshell. The answer hinges on the subscript J (0 vs 2), which is written '^3 P0'/'^3 P2' in the corpus. q: What is a Slater determinant, and why does writing a wavefunction that way automatically satisfy the Pauli principle?
expect: A Slater determinant writes an N-electron wavefunction as a determinant of spin-orbitals (a spatial orbital times spin α or β): each row holds one electron's coordinates and each column one spin-orbital, with normalization constant 1/√(N!). Interchanging two rows (or columns) of a determinant changes its sign, so the wavefunction is antisymmetric to the exchange of any two electrons, as fermions require; and if two columns were the same (two electrons in the same spin-orbital) the determinant would be zero, which is the exclusion principle. For ground-state helium: ψ = (1/√2)|φ1s(1)α(1) φ1s(1)β(1); φ1s(2)α(2) φ1s(2)β(2)| = (1/√2)[φ1s(1)α(1)φ1s(2)β(2) − φ1s(2)α(2)φ1s(1)β(1)]. Expanding an N × N determinant gives N! terms (720 for carbon). One determinant corresponds to one configuration; some states need linear combinations of determinants. Slater introduced it in 1929 (Heisenberg and Dirac used the form three years earlier).
note: Taught in Physical Chemistry 8.6: introduction (lines 113-115), helium determinant (lines 117-123), row/column rule and (N!)^(-1/2) (line 125), general N-electron form (line 129), construction rules and 'anti-symmetric upon exchange of any two electrons' (lines 181-184), carbon's 720 terms (line 222). 9.9 lines 46-60 adds the property list ('If any two columns in a determinant are the same, the determinant is 0'). False positives: 11-1 and 08-7 (Hartree-Fock uses a single determinant, not explained), 11-2 (molecular spin-orbitals in the determinant are built from basis functions), 09-6 (H2 ground state).

q: why are chemists allowed to treat the nuclei as frozen when they work out the electrons in a molecule? what is the Born-Oppenheimer approximation actually doing?
expect: Nuclei are much heavier than electrons (more than 1000 times; 1836 times for a proton), so they move much more slowly and the electrons adjust almost instantly to wherever the nuclei are. The Born-Oppenheimer approximation therefore neglects the nuclear kinetic-energy terms of the molecular Hamiltonian when solving for the electrons: one solves the electronic Schrödinger equation Ĥ_elec φe(r,R) = Ee(R)φe(r,R) with the nuclei held at fixed positions R. The nuclear positions still matter - the electronic wavefunction and energy depend on R - and the total wavefunction is the product ψ = X(R)φe(r,R) of a nuclear (vibrational) and an electronic function. Ee(R) plus the nuclear repulsion gives the potential energy curve V(R) (a surface with 3N−6, or 3N−5 for linear molecules, dimensions in polyatomics) on which the nuclei vibrate: (T̂_nuc + V(R))X = EX. The crude Born-Oppenheimer approximation goes further and fixes R at the equilibrium separation R0.

q: Rank O2+, O2, O2- and O2^2- by bond length. What bond lengths does the book give for them?

q: Using Hückel theory with β ≈ −75 kJ/mol, how big is the delocalization energy of benzene compared with butadiene, and how does benzene's value compare with experiment?
expect: Benzene: the secular determinant has roots x = ±2, ±1, ±1, giving π energies α + 2β, α + β (twice), α − β (twice), α − 2β. Its six π electrons fill the three bonding MOs: E = 2(α + 2β) + 4(α + β) = 6α + 8β. Three localized ethylene double bonds give 3 × 2(α + β) = 6α + 6β, so the delocalization energy is 2β = 2(−75) = −150 kJ/mol, close to the experimental thermochemical value of −152 kJ/mol. Butadiene: roots x = ±0.618, ±1.618, energies α ± 1.618β and α ± 0.618β; four π electrons give E = 2(α + 1.618β) + 2(α + 0.618β) = 4α + 4.472β versus 4α + 4β for two ethylenes, so the delocalization energy is 0.472β ≈ −35 kJ/mol. Benzene's is about four times larger (−25 vs about −8.9 kJ/mol per π electron), the extra stabilization of an aromatic (4n + 2) π system.
note: Physical Chemistry 10.7: roots ±2, ±1, ±1 (line 38), E_tot = 6α + 8β (line 72), ΔE = 2β (lines 78-82), experimental −152 kJ/mol (line 84), Hückel's 4n+2 rule. 10.6: x = ±0.618, ±1.618 (line 73), E1 = α + 1.618β (line 75), Eπ = 4α + 4.472β (line 93), 2 × Eπ(ethylene) = 4α + 4β (line 99), 0.47β and β ≈ −75 kJ/mol giving −35 kJ/mol (line 105; [Note: corrected] at line 107 records the printed 0.48β). The book applies β = −75 kJ/mol only to butadiene; applying it to benzene is the changed number. Arithmetic: 2 × −75 = −150; 0.472 × −75 = −35.4; −150/6 = −25.0; −35.4/4 = −8.85. q: What does the basis set name 6-31G** mean, and how does it differ from 6-31G* and 6-31+G*?
expect: Pople notation N-MPG: '6' means each inner-shell (core, 1s) STO is a contraction of 6 primitive Gaussians; the hyphen marks a split-valence (double-zeta valence) set; '31' means each valence STO is split into an inner part made of 3 primitives (large ζ, the smaller orbital) and an outer part of 1 primitive (small ζ, the larger orbital); G = Gaussian. One asterisk (6-31G*) adds polarization functions - a set of d functions - on the heavier atoms; two asterisks (6-31G**) also add polarization functions (p functions) to the light atoms hydrogen and helium; 6-31G** is synonymous with 6-31G(d,p). A plus sign (6-31+G*) instead adds diffuse functions - very shallow Gaussians that describe the outer 'tail' of the orbitals, important for anions and large 'soft' systems - and ++ adds them to H and He as well.
note: Physical Chemistry 11.2: N-MPG* notation and the asterisk (line 89), '6-31G means each inner shell (1s orbital) STO is a linear combination of 6 primitives and each valence shell STO is split into an inner and outer part (double zeta) using 3 and 1 primitive Gaussians' (line 91), Table 11.2.1 (lines 97-99). 11.3 lines 36-42 (N-MPG, M the smaller orbital, P the larger). 11.4: 'Two asterisks, indicate that polarization functions are also added to light atoms (hydrogen and helium) ... The 6-31G** is synonymous to 6-31 G(d,p)' (line 10), asterisk/p function on H (line 17), diffuse functions '+'/'++' (line 23). Tokens: *, ** and + change the meaning. '6-31G' occurs in 6 files: 11-2, 11-3, 11-4, physchem 10-6 (figure computed at HF/6-31G*), inorgchem 6.4 (a figure caption) and inorgchem 6.5 line 175 ('calculated ... at the 6-31G** level') - the last three use the name without explaining it.

q: Why do quantum chemistry programs build basis sets out of Gaussian functions instead of Slater-type orbitals, and what is a contracted Gaussian?
expect: Slater-type orbitals, with radial part R(r) = N r^(n−1) e^(−ζr), have the right shape: they decay exponentially with distance (good long-range overlap) and peak at the nucleus (the cusp), but the integrals they require are computationally difficult. Gaussian functions, with radial part r^(n−1) e^(−αr^2), make overlap and other integrals much easier to evaluate (Frank Boys' insight), which saves a great deal of computer time. A single Gaussian is a poor orbital, though: it is flat rather than steep at r = 0 and falls off too quickly at large r. So each STO is replaced by a fixed linear combination of several primitive Gaussians with different exponents; this frozen combination, not re-optimized in the variational calculation and treated as a single function, is a contracted Gaussian function. The STO-NG sets are built this way, e.g. STO-3G, where each STO is fitted by three primitive Gaussians (a minimal basis).
note: Physical Chemistry 11.2: STO radial form (line 42), GTO form (line 70), 'flat rather than steep near the atomic nucleus at r = 0, and they fall off more rapidly at large values of r' (line 74), primitive and contracted Gaussians (line 84), STO-NG (Figure 11.2.2 caption), summary crediting Frank Boys and easier integrals (line 124). 11.1 line 88 (contracted Gaussians are composed from primitives to match STOs). 11.3 line 18 (STO-nG minimal sets: STO-3G, STO-4G, STO-6G). Near-misses: 7.2 lines 232-248 (Slater and Gaussian orbitals as LCAO basis functions, no contraction), 11.4 (polarization and diffuse functions), 13.7 (Gaussian form of harmonic-oscillator wavefunctions).

q: Which point groups allow a molecule to have a permanent dipole moment, and in what direction must the dipole point?
expect: Only molecules in the point groups Cn, Cnv and Cs can have a permanent dipole moment. A dipole must lie parallel to any Cn axis: a Cn axis with n > 1 forbids a dipole perpendicular to it (the rotation would reverse it), and an operation that swaps the two ends of the molecule, such as a σh mirror plane or a C2 axis perpendicular to the principal axis, forbids a dipole along the axis. So in Cn and Cnv molecules the dipole lies along the rotation axis (e.g. water, C2v, along its C2 axis).
note: Physical Chemistry 12.2 'Symmetry and Physical Properties' (lines 286-288): 'Any dipole must lie parallel to a Cn axis', the σh / perpendicular-C2 argument, and 'The only groups compatible with a dipole moment are Cn, C_nv and Cs. In molecules belonging to Cn or C_nv the dipole must lie along the axis of rotation.' Water's C2 axis and C2v symmetry: 12.2 line 43 and 13.10 line 24. Only physchem 12.2 states this rule. Near-misses: inorgchem 3.3 (molecular polarity from VSEPR shapes and bond dipoles), inorgchem 4.2 (point-group flowchart, no dipole rule), inorgchem 4.4 and physchem 12.2 line 290 (chirality from symmetry, a different property), physchem 13.12 (a permanent dipole is needed for a rotational spectrum).

q: When group theory is used on water's vibrations in C2v, is the antisymmetric O-H stretch labelled B1 or B2?
expect: The books disagree. Physical Chemistry gives Γ_vib(H2O) = 2a1 + b2: the symmetric stretch (ν1) and the bend (ν2) are a1 and the antisymmetric stretch (ν3) is b2; its Γ_tot = 3a1 + a2 + 2b1 + 3b2, with character 3 under σ(yz), i.e. the molecule is placed in the yz plane (y transforms as b2). Inorganic Chemistry gives Γ_modes = 3A1 + A2 + 3B1 + 2B2 and vibrations 2A1 + B1, calling the antisymmetric stretch B1; its character of 3 is under σv(xz), so the molecule lies in the xz plane. The difference is only the choice of which mirror plane contains the molecule, which swaps the B1 and B2 labels; both books agree that water has three vibrations, two totally symmetric (A1) and one antisymmetric, and that all three are IR- and Raman-active. A good answer reports both labels with the axis convention rather than picking one.

Neither book comments on the other's convention. physchem 12.2 is itself mixed: line 139 says the x axis lies in the plane of the molecule (which would make water's stretch b1), but rule 3 (lines 145-148) puts x perpendicular when z lies in the molecular plane, matching its b2. q: What are water's three fundamental vibrations and their wavenumbers? Do the two O-H stretches have the same frequency?
expect: No. Water (3N − 6 = 3 vibrations) has a symmetric stretch ν1 (a1) at 3657 cm^-1, an asymmetric stretch ν3 (b2) at 3756 cm^-1 and a bend ν2 (a1) at 1595 cm^-1; the two stretching modes differ in both symmetry (a1 vs b2) and energy. By convention for a nonlinear molecule ν1 is the symmetric stretch, ν2 the bend and ν3 the asymmetric stretch. All three modes are IR-active (and Raman-active), so the IR spectrum of water shows three bands, as group theory predicts (Γ_vib = 2a1 + b2; Γ_stretch = a1 + b2, Γ_bend = a1).

q: why is there a gap right in the middle of HCl's infrared spectrum, exactly where the pure vibrational line should be?
expect: HCl's IR band is a rovibrational spectrum: the vibrational change Δv = +1 is accompanied by a rotational change, and because a photon carries one unit of angular momentum the rule is ΔJ = ±1. ΔJ = +1 gives the R branch at hν0 + 2hB(J + 1) (above the band centre) and ΔJ = −1 the P branch at hν0 − 2hBJ (below it). A line at the band centre ν0 itself would need ΔJ = 0 (a Q branch), which is forbidden for diatomics like HCl that have no electronic angular momentum in the ground state, so the pure vibrational transition is missing. That leaves the 'zero gap' between R(0) and P(1), 4B wide, while the other lines are about 2B apart. A Q branch does appear for polyatomic molecules and for diatomics with electronic angular momentum, such as NO.

The [Note: corrected] at line 100 replaces the printed reason ('Most diatomics, such as O2, have a small moment of inertia and thus very small angular momentum and yield no Q-branch') - a model repeating that reason is wrong. q: why can't you build a laser out of atoms that only have two energy levels, no matter how hard you pump them?
expect: Laser light (coherent) comes from stimulated emission, which must outpace absorption: B21ρ(ν)N2 > B12ρ(ν)N1. Since B21 = B12 and the radiation density is the same, this needs N2 > N1, a population inversion. In a two-level atom the pump light drives absorption and stimulated emission with the same B coefficient, so even an arbitrarily strong pump only brings the two populations toward equality (when they are equal, as many atoms go up as come down); a population inversion cannot be achieved by pumping. The fix is a third, metastable level: in a three-level laser such as ruby, the pump excites level 1 → 3, atoms decay quickly 3 → 2 and collect in the long-lived level 2, and if the pump rate out of level 1 exceeds level 2's decay rate, N2 > N1 and the 2 → 1 transition lases. Four-level lasers (He-Ne, Nd:YAG), whose lower laser level is not the ground state, are easier still to pump and to run continuously.
note: Taught in Physical Chemistry 15.3 lines 20-28 (B21 = B12, N2 > N1, 'Population inversion cannot be achieved in a two-level atom by pumping ... Even an arbitrarily strong pump only brings the populations toward equality') and 15.4 lines 10 (optical pumping at most equalizes the populations; a third metastable level), 56 (ruby, with its [Note: corrected] at 58) and 104 (four-level). The [Note: corrected] at 15.3 line 30 records the printed 'not very practical ... It can be done but is very energy costly and inefficient', which a correct answer must not repeat. Instrumental Analysis 7.2 line 78 agrees: a two-level system 'cannot create a population inversion' because at equal populations pumping and emission rates balance. q: In a helium-neon laser, which atoms actually emit the red 632.8 nm light, and what job does the helium do?
expect: Neon emits the laser light; helium is the energy-transfer agent. The He-Ne laser is a four-level gas laser and was the first continuous-wave (cw) laser. An electric discharge (the text says electromagnetic pumping) excites helium into two metastable states, 2^3S (1s2s ^3S1) and 2^1S (1s2s ^1S0), which cannot de-excite by emitting light; instead they pass their energy to neon atoms in collisions, because the energies nearly match: He*(1s2s ^3S1) + Ne → He + Ne*(2p^5 4s) and He*(1s2s ^1S0) + Ne → He + Ne*(2p^5 5s). These Ne 4s and 5s levels are the upper lasing levels; the lower levels (3p and 4p) decay rapidly to the metastable 3s level, so a population inversion is easily achieved. The 632.8 nm line is a 5s → 3p transition (5s ^1P1 → 3p ^3P2 in Table 15.6.1, A = 6.56 × 10^6 s^-1). The gas is about 5 parts He to 1 part Ne in a narrow 2-3 mm bore; typical output is a few mW at an overall efficiency near 0.1%.

q: What is the Boltzmann factor, and what does it tell you?
expect: The Boltzmann factor is e^(−βE_i), where E_i is the energy of state i and β = 1/kT (T the kelvin temperature, k the Boltzmann constant). The probability that a system is in a state j of energy E_j falls off exponentially with that energy, as e^(−E_j/kT), so low-energy states are the most populated and kT (the thermal energy, E_thermal = kT) sets the energy scale. It is used to approximate the fraction of particles in a large system with a given energy, and it governs activation processes: raising T lets more particles cross an energy barrier, and the fraction of molecules with enough energy to cross it is approximately proportional to the Boltzmann factor.
note: Physical Chemistry 17.1: E_thermal = kT (line 69), the Boltzmann factor e^(−βEi) (line 73) with β = 1/kT (line 83), and activation processes 'approximately proportional to the Boltzmann factor' (line 85). 17.2 line 18: the probability pj 'falls off exponentially with the energy of state j, as e^(−Ej/kT)' (a [Note] corrects the printed 'is exponentially proportional to'). DISTRACTOR: 'Boltzmann' appears in 38 files across physchem and analchem, and 'Boltzmann factor' in 10 (17-1 to 17-8, 18-3, 18-6), but only 17-1 and 17-2 say what it is. Likely false positives: 27-3 (Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution), 20-5 (S = k ln W), 17-3 to 17-8 (partition functions built from the factor), and analchem 08-1, 10-1 and 19-1, which apply the Boltzmann distribution to excited-state or nuclear-spin populations (correct but narrower).

q: why do we divide the partition function by N! for a gas but not for the molecules in a crystal? isn't a molecule a molecule
expect: For distinguishable, independent molecules, such as molecules in a molecular crystal that can be told apart by their fixed lattice sites, the system partition function is just the product of the molecular ones, Q = q^N. In a gas the molecules are indistinguishable, so swapping them gives no new state; using q^N would count each state up to N! times (the N! permutations of the molecules), so Q = q^N/N!. The book's two-particle, two-level example shows the overcount: distinguishable particles give four states (e^0 + 2e^(−βε) + e^(−2βε) = q^2), indistinguishable ones only three. The N! correction assumes no two particles occupy the same state, so it is valid only when the number of accessible molecular states greatly exceeds N (as it does for a gas).
note: Physical Chemistry 17.6 line 18 (molecules in a molecular crystal are distinguishable by position) and line 40 (Q = [q(V, β)]^N). 17.7 lines 20-42: the two-particle example (Q_distinguishable = q^2; indistinguishable Q = e^0 + e^(−βε) + e^(−2βε) ≠ q^2, line 34), 'N! permutations' and Q = q^N/N! (line 42); line 46 plus the [Note] at line 48 give the validity condition (states greatly exceed N; the source's 'only applicable for large N' is corrected). Tests a conceptual why-question in casual phrasing. Likely false positives: 17-5, 18-3, 18-7 and 26-8, which use q^N/N! (or Stirling's ln N!) without explaining it, and 20-1 (Stirling's approximation).

q: In the rotational partition function q_rot = T/(σΘ_rot), what is σ? Use it to get q_rot for N2 and for HCl at 300 K.
expect: σ is the symmetry number: the number of distinct rotations that bring the molecule into an indistinguishable configuration; dividing by it corrects the overcounting of rotational states. A homonuclear diatomic (N2) has σ = 2 (a 180° rotation gives the same configuration); a heteronuclear one (HCl) has σ = 1. With Θ_rot = 2.88 K for N2 and 15.2 K for HCl: q_rot(N2) = 300/(2 × 2.88) ≈ 52.1 and q_rot(HCl) = 300/(1 × 15.2) ≈ 19.7. For polyatomics σ = 1 for linear molecules without a center of symmetry (HCN), 2 with one (CO2), 2 for H2O and NO2, 3 for NH3 and 12 for CH4.
note: Physical Chemistry 18.6 line 58 defines the symmetry number ('equal to the distinct number of ways by which a molecule can be brought into identical configurations by rotations'), line 66 q_rot = T/(Θ_rot σ), Table 1 line 36 (N2 2.88, HCl 15.2), and Example 18.6.1 uses σ = 2 for H2 (q_rot = 1.713, line 86). 18.8 line 135 lists σ for polyatomics. q: why does the measured heat capacity of hydrogen gas at low temperature not match what you calculate for H2 at equilibrium? something about ortho and para?
expect: H2 exists as ortho-hydrogen (nuclear spins parallel, triplet nuclear spin state, combined with odd J rotational levels) and para-hydrogen (spins antiparallel, singlet, even J), because the total wavefunction must be antisymmetric under exchange of the two spin-1/2 protons. At high temperature the ortho:para ratio is 3 (3:1, i.e. 0.75/0.25); at equilibrium at low temperature it goes to 0 (all para). But ortho → para interconversion is very slow, so when H2 is cooled the ratio stays frozen at the high-temperature 3:1 value. The measured rotational heat capacity therefore matches C_V = (3/4)C_V(ortho) + (1/4)C_V(para), a 'frozen high-temperature mixture', not the equilibrium curve; with a catalyst such as activated charcoal the experiment does follow the equilibrium (eq) curve.
note: Physical Chemistry 18.10: ortho/para definitions (line 10), q_ortho (odd J, weight 3) and q_para (even J, weight 1) (lines 67-71), high-T limit No/Np = 3 and → 0 as T → 0 (line 85), the 3:1 experimental curve (Figure 18.10.1, lines 103-108; a [Note] corrects the caption), C_V = (3/4)ortho + (1/4)para (line 110) and the frozen mixture / activated charcoal explanation (line 112). Only this section covers nuclear-spin isomers of H2. q: 1.50 mol of an ideal gas at 298 K expands into an evacuated space, from 10.0 L to 30.0 L. No heat flows and no work is done, so is ΔS zero? Find ΔS for the gas, the surroundings and the universe.
expect: No. In the expansion against vacuum q = 0, w = 0 and ΔU = 0, but q_irr = 0 cannot be used to get ΔS. Because S is a state function, compute ΔS along a reversible isothermal path between the same states: q_rev = nRT ln(V2/V1), so ΔS_sys = nR ln(V2/V1) = (1.50 mol)(8.314 J/(mol·K)) ln(30.0/10.0) = 13.7 J/K. Nothing happens in the surroundings, so ΔS_surr = 0 and ΔS_total = +13.7 J/K (positive, so the expansion is spontaneous). For comparison, a reversible isothermal expansion has the same ΔS_sys but ΔS_surr = −13.7 J/K, so ΔS_total = 0.
note: Physical Chemistry 20.6 'Vacuum Expansion': ∫−P_ext dV = 0 (line 24), 'No energy and no work means no heat!' (line 28), q_rev = nRT ln(V2/V1) and ΔS = nR ln(V2/V1) (line 40), 'As S is a state function this equation also holds for the irreversible expansion against vacuum' (line 42), ΔS_total = nR ln(V2/V1) + 0 (line 50), and the reversible case summing to zero. q: if i built a perfect frictionless engine running off geyser water at 400 K and dumped the waste heat into a 300 K river, why couldn't it turn all the heat into work? what's the best it could do?
expect: The second law limits the conversion of heat into work. For a reversible Carnot engine the efficiency is η = |w|/q_h = 1 − T_c/T_h (because q_c/q_h = −T_c/T_h for the cycle, as ∮dS = 0). With T_h = 400 K and T_c = 300 K, η = 1 − 300/400 = 25%: at best a quarter of the heat becomes work and three quarters is dumped into the river, and real engines do worse because of friction and other losses. Full efficiency would need T_c = 0 K, which is never reached, and if T_c = T_h no work can be obtained at all.

The [Note] at line 92 records that the source prints '= 24%'; 1 − 0.75 = 0.25, so a correct answer says 25%. 'Carnot' occurs only in this file. q: if the third law says entropy is zero at absolute zero, how come solid carbon monoxide still has entropy left over near 0 K?
expect: The third law gives S = 0 at 0 K only for a pure, perfect crystal with a single lowest-energy arrangement (W = 1, so S = k ln W = 0). In solid CO the C and O ends are similar in size and the dipole is weak, so molecules can freeze in either orientation (C≡O or O≡C) with nearly the same energy. The disorder set in when the crystal formed is never removed on cooling because the ordering is extremely slow (kinetically frozen in). If each molecule has 2 orientations, W = 2^N and S_disorder = k ln 2^N = Nk ln 2 = R ln 2 ≈ 5.7 J/(mol·K) per mole; the measured residual entropy is about 4.4 J/(mol·K), smaller because the two orientations are not exactly equal in energy. This residual entropy shows up as a gap between the spectroscopically calculated and the calorimetric entropy (S_calc − S_exp); ice and glasses show it too. It is an exception to the perfect-crystal premise, not a contradiction of the third law.
note: Physical Chemistry 21.2: third law for a perfect crystal, S = k ln W with W = 1 (line 55 onward); 'Residual Entropy in Carbon Monoxide' (line 98): orientations nearly isoenergetic, Nk ln 2 = 5.7 J/(mol K) (line 104), ordering kinetics extremely slow (line 106), experimental ≈ 4.4 J/(mol K) (line 108), and the Summary. 21.8 lines 10-14: residual entropy = S̄_calc − S̄_exp, glass, ice and CO; the [Note] at line 16 corrects the source's 'must still have zero entropy according to third law'. Arithmetic: R ln 2 = 8.3145 × 0.6931 = 5.76 J/(mol K). Likely false positives: 20-5 (S = k ln W in general; the old q096 asks what W and k are), 21-5/21-6 (calorimetric vs statistical absolute entropies without CO), 21-1 (entropy rising with temperature).

q: How does the heat capacity of a crystalline solid depend on temperature very close to absolute zero, and is it different for a metal?
expect: Near 0 K the heat capacity is not constant (as the classical Dulong–Petit law assumes) but falls sharply, because only low-frequency vibrational modes (phonons) are thermally accessible. The Debye model gives C_P = aT^3 at low temperatures. For a metal the conduction electrons add a term linear in T, so C_P = aT + bT^3: the aT term is the electronic contribution and the bT^3 term comes from the lattice vibrations of the Debye model.
note: Physical Chemistry 21.4: Debye model vs Dulong–Petit and phonons (line 10), C_P = aT^3 (line 12), metals C_P = aT + bT^3 (line 18) with the aT term from conduction electrons and bT^3 from lattice vibrations (line 22). 17.4 covers Dulong–Petit (C_V = 3R) and Einstein's model, where C_V → 0 as T → 0 exponentially (not T^3); it is a near miss, not the answer to the low-T law. q: What are the natural variables of the Helmholtz energy A and of the Gibbs energy G, and which one is the criterion for spontaneity at constant T and V?
expect: A ≡ U − TS, so dA = −PdV − SdT and the natural variables of A are V and T: A(V, T). G ≡ H − TS = A + PV, so dG = VdP − SdT and its natural variables are P and T: G(P, T). At constant V and T, dA ≤ 0: A decreases for a spontaneous process and is constant at equilibrium; at constant T and P the criterion is dG ≤ 0. (For comparison U(S, V) and H(S, P).) G is the more useful in the lab because P and T are the usual experimental variables.

EXACT TOKEN: the bare symbol 'A' is ambiguous in the corpus: absorbance A (analchem, Beer's law), area A (16-1 P = F/A), mass number A, and reactant 'A' in every kinetics section (28-x, 29-x). The answer must tie A to the Helmholtz energy and not confuse its variables with G's (a common error is to give G(V, T)).

q: What is fugacity, and what does the fugacity coefficient tell you about a real gas?
expect: Fugacity f is an 'effective pressure' introduced (by G. N. Lewis, 1901) so that the ideal-gas form dḠ = RT d ln P can be used for any substance: dḠ = RT d ln f, i.e. μ = μ° + RT ln(f/P°). For an ideal gas f = P. The fugacity coefficient is the ratio f/P (written φ in 22.8, γ in 26.10, f = γp); it equals 1 for ideal behaviour and is a measure of non-ideality: the closer to 1, the more ideal the gas. All gases approach ideality as P → 0, so f → P there. It can be found from the compression factor: ln γ = ∫0^p (Z − 1)/p dp. At equilibrium, fugacities replace partial pressures in K.
note: Physical Chemistry 22.8: Lewis 1901 (line 26; a [Note] at line 28 corrects the printed 1905), dḠ = RT d ln f (line 30), φ = f/P (line 34), φ = 1 for ideal gas and 'regarded as a measure of non-ideality' (line 36), zero-pressure limit (line 38), μ̄ = μ̄° + RT ln(f/P°). 26.10: f = γp (line 46), ln γ = ∫0^p ((Z − 1)/p)_T dp (line 66), γ = 1 for an ideal gas and as p → 0 (line 68). Note the two sections use different symbols (φ vs γ) for the same coefficient, and γ is also the activity coefficient in 24-7, 25-5 and 26-11/26-12. Likely false positives: analchem 22-3 (standard potential at 'unit fugacity', no definition), 24-7/24-8/25-2 (activities of solutions), 26-2 (mentions fugacity coefficients changing K).

q: What are the temperature and pressure of water's triple point? Is that the same as its normal melting point?
expect: The triple point is the only point where solid, liquid and vapour are all in equilibrium (where the three phase-boundary lines meet). For water it is at 273.16 K and only 4.58 Torr. It is not the normal melting point (273.15 K) but differs from it by only 0.01 K, because the solid-liquid line is almost vertical (and for water it leans slightly backwards: water expands on freezing, so its melting point drops a little with pressure).

q: how do you measure rate constants for a reaction that's basically over before you can even mix the reactants, like H3O+ + OH- recombining?
expect: Use a relaxation method. Flow methods (continuous, stopped or quenched flow) only reach the millisecond range, so for faster reactions start with the system already at equilibrium and perturb it suddenly, e.g. by a temperature jump (or use a light flash, flash photolysis, to create a reactive species in situ). After the jump the old composition is no longer the equilibrium one (an endothermic A ⇌ B shifts toward B on heating, by Le Chatelier), and the displacement from the new equilibrium decays exponentially: Δ[B] = Δ[B]0 e^(−(k1 + k−1)t) = Δ[B]0 e^(−t/τ). The relaxation time τ = 1/(k1 + k−1) is the time for the displacement to fall to 1/e of its initial value, and a plot of ln(Δ[B]/Δ[B]0) vs t is a straight line of slope −(k1 + k−1), giving the rate constants at the new temperature. The H3O+ + OH− recombination and I− + I2 → I3− are the book's classic examples.
note: Physical Chemistry 28.6: flow methods (continuous, stopped flow line 27, quenched flow), relaxation methods and flash photolysis (line 58), the fast reactions H3O+ + OH− → 2H2O (line 82; [Notes] at lines 80 and 84 correct the printed 'dissociation of water') and I− + I2 → I3− (line 88), temperature jumps (line 92) with the Le Chatelier shift (line 98), relaxation time defined as the time for Δx to fall to Δx/e (line 106; a [Note] corrects the printed 'half-time'), and the derivation ending in Δ[B] = Δ[B]0 e^{−(k1 + k−1)t} = Δ[B]0 e^(−t/τ) and the ln plot of slope −(k1 + k−1) (lines 152-154). The section gives the sum k1 + k−1 but does not say how to separate the two constants, so the expect does not claim it. Likely false positives: 28-5 (reversible reactions, qualitative), analchem 19-1 (NMR 'relaxation time', unrelated), physchem 15-x (laser rate equations), 29-2 (detailed balance).

q: What does transition state theory give for a rate constant, and why is the TST value always an upper bound on the true rate constant?
expect: Transition state theory places a dividing surface at the transition state (q = q‡) and counts the flux of trajectories crossing it toward products, giving k_TST = (k_B T/h) e^(−βΔF‡) = (k_B T/h) e^(−(F‡ − F_r)/k_B T), where ΔF‡ is the free energy of the transition state relative to the reactants (the same form as k = (RT/Nh) e^(−ΔG‡/RT) used in inorganic kinetics, since R/N = k_B). TST assumes every trajectory that starts across the dividing surface toward products ends as product. In reality some trajectories recross and return to reactants, so the true rate constant is k = κ k_TST with a transmission factor κ < 1: the reactive-flux function k(t) starts at k_TST at t = 0 and decays to a lower plateau, so k_TST is always an upper bound.
note: Physical Chemistry 28.8: TST assumptions, k(t) and k^(TST) = k(0); final result k^(TST) = ((kB T)/h)e^(−βΔF‡) (line 94); Figure 28.8.2 and 'k^(TST) is always an upper bound to the true rate constant' (line 96); k = κk^(TST) (line 103) with 'the factor κ < 1 ... known as the transmission factor' for recrossings (line 105). Inorganic Chemistry 12.3 line 528 gives k = (RT/Nh)e^{−(ΔG‡)/RT} (the same expression per mole) but says nothing about κ or recrossing, so it answers only the first half. q: methyl isocyanide just rearranges to acetonitrile, one molecule on its own, so how can its rate law be second order at low pressure?
expect: The Lindemann (Christiansen–Lindemann, Lindemann–Hinshelwood) mechanism: a molecule must first be energized by a collision, A + M ⇌ A* + M (k1, k−1), and only then does the energized A* react, A* → B (k2); there is a time delay during which A* can be deactivated by another collision. The steady-state approximation for A* gives rate = k_obs[A] with k_obs = k1k2[M]/(k2 + k−1[M]). At high pressure collisions are frequent, k−1[M] ≫ k2, and rate = (k1k2/k−1)[A], first order. At low pressure collisions are rare, k−1[M] ≪ k2, so every activation leads to product and rate = k1[A][M]; with M = CH3NC itself this is second order, −d[CH3NC]/dt = k[CH3NC]^2, as observed.
note: Physical Chemistry 29.6: Three Principles of the Lindemann Mechanism (line 65), CH3NC → CH3CN first order 'only observed at high pressures', second order at low pressure (line 113), Christiansen and Lindemann's energization step (line 117), k_obs = (k1 k2[M])/(k2 + k−1[M]) (line 139), high-pressure limit (line 141) and low-pressure limit (line 147); the N2O5 example and its [Note] on the limit conditions are earlier in the file. Only this file mentions Lindemann. Not the old q078 (rate law from coefficients) or q080 (NO2 + CO mechanism).

q: What is the steady-state approximation in kinetics? Does 'steady state' mean the reaction has stopped?
expect: It is applied to a highly reactive, short-lived intermediate I whose concentration stays small (much smaller than that of the species that set the rate) and nearly constant, so one sets d[I]/dt ≈ 0. That turns the differential equation for [I] into an algebraic one: solve it for [I] and substitute into the rate of product formation. Example: for A + A → A2 (k1), A2 + B → C + A (k2), d[A2]/dt = k1[A]^2 − k2[A2][B] ≈ 0 gives [A2] = k1[A]^2/(k2[B]) and d[C]/dt = k1[A]^2, second order in A. No, the reaction has not stopped: the 'state' that is approximately steady is the intermediate's concentration (it reacts about as fast as it forms), not the state of the system, which keeps changing because a net reaction is occurring.
note: Physical Chemistry 29.4 line 10 (highly reactive intermediate, d[I]/dt = 0) and the worked mechanisms to d[C]/dt = k1[A]^2 (line 46) and k1[A]; 29.5 lines 132-136 (intermediate's concentration much smaller, slope negligible; 'the "state" which is approximately "steady" is the concentration of the intermediate, not the state of the system'); Inorganic Chemistry 12.1 line 76 (an intermediate 'is assumed to react as quickly as it forms'). q: in crossed molecular beam experiments, why does the DF from F + D2 fly back the way the F came from, while the KI from K + I2 keeps going forward?
expect: F + D2 → DF + D is a rebound reaction: most DF molecules bounce back toward the direction from which the F atom approached the collision (some straight back). K + I2 is a stripping reaction: an electron transfers from K to I2 before the particles actually collide (K + I2 → K+ + I2−), the Coulomb attraction between the ions draws them together (K+ + I2− → KI + I), and the KI moves off in the same general direction as the incoming K atom. Because the electron jumps at long range, the experimental cross-section of stripping reactions is larger than the hard-sphere estimate. A third type forms a meta-stable complex that rotates many times before breaking up, scattering products both forward and backward.
note: Physical Chemistry 30.8 line 96: most DF 'head back towards the direction from which the F atom originally approached ... This type of collision is called a rebound reaction.' 30.9: stripping reactions defined (line 10), cross-section larger than the hard-sphere estimate and electron transfer before the collision (line 18), K(g) + I2(g) → K+(g) + I2−(g), then KI(g) + I(g) (lines 20-22), KI moving off 'in the same general direction as the incoming K atom' (line 24), meta-stable intermediates scattering forward and backward (line 26). q: What's the difference between physisorption and chemisorption?
expect: In physisorption (e.g. Ar on metals) the only attraction is weak van der Waals forces, giving a shallow potential-energy minimum at a relatively large distance from the surface (typically d > 0.3 nm); there is no barrier, so it is not activated and its kinetics are invariably fast. In chemisorption a chemical bond forms between adsorbate and surface, giving a much deeper minimum at a shorter distance (d_ch < d_ph); the depth of this well is the energy of adsorption ΔE_ads (negative; the heat of adsorption Q = −ΔH_ads is positive). Molecular chemisorption may have no barrier, while dissociative chemisorption can be activated or non-activated depending on where the physisorption and chemisorption curves cross; desorption always has a barrier, Ea(des) ≈ −ΔH_ads.
note: Physical Chemistry 31.6: Figure 31.6.2 caption 'd_ph is always greater than d_ch' (line 33); CASE I Physisorption (line 41): weak van der Waals forces, shallow minimum, d > 0.3 nm (line 43), 'not activated ... invariably fast' (line 48); CASE II (line 50): 'much deeper chemisorption minimum at shorter values of d' (line 52), well depth = energy of adsorption (line 69), heat of adsorption Q = −ΔH(ads) (line 73); CASE III dissociative chemisorption (line 90), activated or non-activated by curve crossing (line 136), Ea(des) ≈ −ΔH_ads (line 151).
